content.content:
---
type: Identity Profile
title: "Runtime Contract"
description: "The load order for every writing job, and the checks that run after."
created: 2026-08-22
updated: 2026-09-25
---

# Runtime Contract

> **Purpose:** This file says which rules load, in what order, and which checks run at the end.
> It is the only file that answers "what was applied to this draft". Read it first, every time.
> Adapted from the runtime contract in [Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer](https://github.com/Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer).
> The architecture is theirs. The rules and the voice are mine.

## Always loaded

Six files load for every piece of writing, on every channel, in this order.

1. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, this file. The load order and the checks.
2. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`. The failure patterns a regex cannot see.
3. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/write-simply.md`. The plain style, and the test for whether the ideas are right.
4. `DIGITAL TWIN/World.md`. The villain, the vision, and what the piece is for.
5. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`. The bar the insight clears before a word is drafted.
6. `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`. How the writing sounds.

Files 2 and 3 are a pair. The pattern rules say what to remove, and `write-simply.md` says what to
aim for, so a draft that only obeys the first one reads stripped.

`World.md` decides what the piece argues and `Voice.md` decides how it sounds, so the two never
collide. Name the skill-tree node before you draft a line. A piece that advances no node is an
idea, so send it back to `SUBSTACK/0_IDEAS/`.

`net-new-value.md` is the guiding principle for all content, on every channel. Write the core
insight as one sentence and name its box before you draft. Only box 4 ships: non-obvious to the
reader and tactical enough to use today. A piece outside box 4 gets one upgrade, then goes back to
the idea bank.

`SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` holds the banned words, phrases and punctuation. `DIGITAL TWIN/rules/`
holds the prose rules, one file each. The `core` rules load into every session through the generated
block in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so you never copy them into another file.

The `craft` rules load for every writing job. Run this once per session before the first draft:

```bash
python SCRIPTS/slop/rules_prompt.py --profile craft
```

## Loaded on demand

One more file loads, chosen by the job. Never load two.

| The job | Load this |
|---|---|
| A Substack article, an essay, a long piece | `DIGITAL TWIN/Long-Form Writing Rules.md` |
| A tutorial, a how-to, a README, developer docs | `DIGITAL TWIN/Technical Writing Style Guide.md` |
| A LinkedIn post, a Note, a tweet, a caption | nothing extra. The channel skill carries it |

`DIGITAL TWIN/AI Writing Policy.md` outranks all of the above and it changes rarely, so read it
when you start a writing session and not once per draft.

## Then the channel skill

The skill carries the shape of the channel and nothing else. It never restates a banned word, a
voice rule or a craft rule, because a copy goes stale and then two files disagree.

| Channel | Skill |
|---|---|
| LinkedIn post | `.claude/skills/write-linkedin-posts/SKILL.md` |
| X post or thread | `.claude/skills/banger-tweets/SKILL.md` |
| Substack Note | `.claude/skills/substack-notes/SKILL.md` |
| Substack article | `.claude/skills/substack-writer/SKILL.md` |
| Reddit post | none. `SOCIALS/Reddit/README.md` is the channel spec |
| Landing page or sales email | `.claude/skills/write-sales-copy/SKILL.md` |
| A stuck idea with no shape yet | `.claude/skills/write-outline/SKILL.md` |
| An existing draft that reads like AI | `.claude/skills/deslop-audit/SKILL.md` |

## Precedence, higher wins

Four layers can disagree. Resolve upward.

1. The banned lists in `slop_rules.py` and the patterns in `core/pattern-rules.md`.
2. The channel skill.
3. `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`.
4. A sample Atharva pastes in the current session.

A sample beats the profile. The profile beats the skill. Two rules never override anything above
them. The fabrication rule below, and the five principles in `AI Writing Policy.md`.

## The fabrication rule

Add no fact that Atharva did not supply. That covers a name, a number, a date, a statistic, a
quote, a source, an event and a client. This rule bites hardest on a rewrite, because the fix for
a vague sentence looks like a specific sentence, and the specifics are not yours to invent.

You have three legal moves when a sentence needs a real detail.

1. Ask him for it.
2. Mark the gap in visible brackets, such as `[the real number]`. Brackets cannot ship by accident.
3. Drop the claim to the level the evidence supports, or cut it.

An invented specific that reads well is a worse defect than the vague sentence it replaced. A
reader cannot catch it.

## The two-pass loop

Never hand over a first draft.

**Pass 1.** Write it. Do not judge while you write.

**Pass 2.** Read it cold and answer five questions for yourself, in writing. Do not print the
answers unless he asks.

1. If a reader called this AI, which exact sentence would they point at?
2. Does the draft carry a fact, a name, a number or a source that he did not give me?
3. Which sentence is the weakest, and does the piece rest on it?
4. Which sentence reads worst, and is the idea under it wrong rather than the wording?
5. Is the core insight still box 4 in `core/net-new-value.md`, or did the draft sand it down to box 2?

**Pass 3.** Fix what the answers found. Then run the checks.

## Announce the load order

Render this panel above every draft. Do not type it by hand.

```bash
python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill <channel skill> --file "<path>"     --node "<the skill-tree node this piece advances>"     --topic "<the idea, for the pillar check>"     --season "<NN beat N, or none>" --format "<number and name, or n/a>"     --insight "<the box 4 insight, one sentence>"
```

`--glob "<pattern>"` replaces `--file` for a batch, and reports the worst result
across the set. `--plain` drops to ASCII. `--technical` swaps the on-demand file
for the Technical Writing Style Guide. The script exits 1 when any measured check
failed, so a caller can gate on it.

```
╭─ LOAD ORDER ─────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ ✓ 1  core/runtime-contract              always               │
│ ✓ 2  core/pattern-rules                 always               │
│ ✓ 3  core/write-simply                  always               │
│ ✓ 4  World.md                           always               │
│ ✓ 5  core/net-new-value                 always               │
│ ✓ 6  Voice.md                           always               │
│ ✓ 7  Long-Form Writing Rules.md         on demand            │
│ ✓ 8  skill:substack-writer              channel              │
├─ WORLD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ villain  rented work                                         │
│ node     builds a gate that refuses bad work                 │
│ season   01 beat 3      format  05 Contrarian Take           │
│ insight  a hook that returns decision: block stops the save  │
├─ CHECKS, measured ───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ✓ pillar      ON (AI)                                        │
│ ✓ slop        CRIT 0                                         │
│ ✓ clarity     CRIT 0                                         │
│ ✓ craft       0                                              │
│ ✓ seo         CRIT 0                                         │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

The two halves carry different weight, and the difference is the point.

**The top half is declared.** You state the node, the season and the box 4 insight. The chain itself
comes from the channel table inside the script, so it cannot drift from this file.

**The bottom half is measured.** The script runs each scorer and prints what it
returned. A tick means a check ran and passed. A cross means it ran and failed. A
dot means the scorer could not run, which never reads as a pass.

That split is why the panel replaced the four hand-typed lines it used to be. A
typed line could claim `slop CRIT 0` for a check nobody ran, which is the blind
spot this contract exists to close. A rendered line cannot.

A missing panel means the chain was skipped.

## The checks, in this order

Run them in order. A later check on a draft that fails an earlier one wastes both your time and his.

| Order | Command | Bar |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Name the box in `core/net-new-value.md` for the one-sentence insight | Box 4. Every channel |
| 0b | The opening gate in `LIBRARY/Resources/Post Uniqueness Check.md` | The top-ranked of 5 openings ships, and no hook is a question. LinkedIn, X, Notes |
| 1 | `python SCRIPTS/pillars/pillars.py --text "<the idea>"` | ON, or an honest BEND |
| 2 | `python SCRIPTS/substack/overlap.py check "<the idea>"` | WRITE. Articles only |
| 3 | `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"` | CRIT reaches 0 |
| 4 | `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"` | CRIT reaches 0. Every channel |
| 5 | `python SCRIPTS/socials/li_format.py "<file>"` | CRIT reaches 0. LinkedIn only |
| 6 | `python SCRIPTS/substack/craft.py "<file>"` | 0. Articles only |
| 7 | `python SCRIPTS/seo/score.py "<file>" --write` | 0. Articles only |
| 8 | `python SCRIPTS/socials/coverage.py` | no `source_blog` warning. Social files only |
| 9 | `python SCRIPTS/review/build.py` | the desk carries it. Every draft is on it, nothing to stamp |

Rows 4, 5 and 6 were missing from this table until 2026-09-04. All three existed
and two of them already blocked a commit, so the table was the only place that
disagreed. A check absent from this file gets skipped by anyone who trusts it,
which is the whole reason the file exists. Add a row here in the same commit
that adds a scorer.

Checks 0, 0b, 1 and 2 run before you draft. Checks 3 to 9 run after. Skip a row only when the row says
so, and say in the announcement block which rows you skipped.

MED and LOW findings from the scorer are advisory. On short-form, ignore its flow, paragraph and
fragment findings, because those rules were written for long-form.

---
type: Draft Article
seo_title: "I Gave an Agent 4 Quickstarts. Here Is What Broke."
seo_description: "The worst bug I found at neatHack sat in my own agent. A model-free rerun in a fresh container now decides what counts as verified."
created: 2026-10-12
updated: 2026-10-12
url_slug: "agent-4-quickstarts-what-broke"
category: "Tech and AI"
cover: ../_COVERS/agent-4-quickstarts-what-broke-cover.png
planned_date: 2026-10-14
goal: "authority"
target_keywords: ["agent quickstarts", "verify AI agent fixes", "quickstart testing", "docs testing agent", "neatHack"]
target_audience: "Docs and DevRel engineers who run an AI agent on their own docs"
core_message: "An agent's fix counts as verified only when a model-free re-run in a fresh container passes, so the check cannot flatter itself."
target_length: "1,800 to 2,000 words"
ai_slop_score: 31
seo_score: 1
---

`jafgen --years 6` fails with `No such option: --years`. That is step 10 of the dbt DuckDB guide, run in a clean container on 10 October 2026. The guide was broken on the day it merged.

FirstRun found that break. FirstRun is the agent I built solo at neatHack, the neatlogs hackathon, to test agent quickstarts and docs. It runs a quickstart in a fresh container, finds the first broken step, and proves the fix with a second clean run.

The docs bugs were the easy part. The harder bugs sat inside my agent, and its own reports hid them. Trusting an agent's report on itself is vibes, which means using a tool without checking its output. So FirstRun runs on one rule. A fix counts as verified only when a model-free rerun in a fresh container passes.

In short:

- neatlogs raised an incident against my agent, at 52.8 times the baseline.
- A planner fix from neatlogs Investigate cut invented steps from 2 of 4 runs to 0 of 52.
- The verify step blocks every model call, so the agent cannot grade its own fix.
- A bisect named jafgen 0.4.6 as the release that broke the dbt guide.
- FirstRun fixed 16 docs pages, and contribution rules held back 3 PRs.

## FirstRun Reads, Plans, Runs, Fixes and Proves

Each run is one loop with five parts.

1. **Read.** Firecrawl pulls the docs page.
2. **Plan.** A Claude planner copies the shell commands into steps.
3. **Run.** Each step runs in a fresh `python:3.11-slim` container.
4. **Fix.** Recovery classes a failure and patches the command, with 3 attempts at most per step.
5. **Prove.** A second container reruns the patched steps with no model calls.

Each run is one neatlogs trace, with a span for each part, so a bad run shows where it went wrong.

## Version 1 Passed Steps That Proved Nothing

I ran v1 on 4 quickstarts with recovery off. Several of its passes were fake.

- A placeholder passed as a step. Chroma step 2 was `true`, a command that does nothing and exits 0.
- A fake secret passed too. `export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'` exits 0 and proves nothing.
- The planner skipped the steps that need an API key, which are the steps most likely to break.
- The plan changed between runs. The same neatlogs page gave 4 steps, then 3 steps, 5 minutes later.
- 9 of 16 steps checked only the exit code, so an error that exits 0 would pass.

Each mistake made the agent's report look better than the run was.

## An Incident Report Named My Agent as the Cause

neatlogs raised an incident on FirstRun itself. It counted 25 "Execution Failed" detections against a baseline of 0.5. That is a 52.8x spike across 10 traces.

The investigation named a root cause at 66% confidence, which neatlogs labels medium. A step ran a `cd` such as `cd my-project`, and the file check after it looked from the old folder. So the agent failed steps that worked.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109215478694441214

Commit 2de852f is the fix, and it changed two things. A file check now looks from the folder where the step started. Every step also runs with `set -e` now. dbt step 3 is five lines, and its failed `pip install` passed on the exit code of the last line.

MkDocs went from a false fail at 14:58 IST to verified 9 of 10 at 15:40 IST.

> **Watch out:** A last line that exits 0 says nothing about the four lines above it. Run every multi-line step with `set -e`.

## A Second Investigation Caught the Planner Inventing Steps

At 14:10 IST I made two neatlogs detections. A detection is a saved rule that flags matching spans. One of them, "planner invented a step", flagged the planner spans of 3 v1 runs.

neatlogs Investigate traced the invented steps to the planner prompt. It proposed a stricter prompt that copies only the commands the docs write.

A headless Claude Code session read the detection over the neatlogs MCP server, the interface an agent uses to query neatlogs. It applied the fix in commit 3ca6f11. Real invented steps fell from 2 of 4 v1 runs to 0 of 52 runs after the fix.

## The Verify Step Blocks Every Model Call

The model that patched a step does not get to judge the patch.

`verify.py` applies the patches and starts a new container. It runs every step inside `config.block_model_calls()`, where any Claude or Jev call raises `ModelCallBlocked`. The run ends `verified` only when every runnable step passes.

A test guards the guard. `tests/test_verify.py` fails if `verify.py` imports the planner, the recovery code or the LLM module.

On the Entire install, recovery added curl and a `PATH` line. Then a fresh container ran all 4 steps with no model calls.

The rule has a limit. A neatlogs AI judge scored 52 runs on 11 October. It agreed with the reported failed step in 46. Only 34 had every patch backed by a passing verify rerun. Runs that stopped before the clean rerun got no proof, and the judge marked them down.

## The Agent Asks a Human Once, Then Remembers

The idea came from Ajay, @bettersayAJ, who wrote "self-healing is self-defeating". So recovery classes each failure before it patches. It checks `precedents.json` first. A precedent is a stored error signature with its class, such as docs bug or environment. A match returns the class at probability 1.0, with no model call.

A new error goes to Jev, a model that returns a typed judgement with a probability. Below 0.7 confidence, FirstRun asks the human one question. The answer goes into `precedents.json`, so the same error never asks again.

https://twitter.com/i/web/status/2108947112809378291

## Bisect Named the Release That Broke the DuckDB Guide

`firstrun bisect` finds when a step broke. It binary-searches a package's releases, one fresh container per probe, with the version pinned.

On the dbt guide, `jafgen --years 6` passes on jafgen 0.3.1, released 2023-01-17. It fails on 0.4.6, released 2024-04-07. PyPI has no release between them. The guide merged on 2025-03-14, 11 months later, so it never worked in a clean environment.

The bisect took 5 probes and $0 in model calls, because it replays stored commands. The table went up as a comment on dbt PR #10149.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109577567103525016

FirstRun opened 4 PRs on day one, each from a verified run.

- [dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149) fixes the removed `jafgen --years` flag.
- [dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10150](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10150) states the Python 3.12 floor the guide needs.
- [entireio/cli#2724](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2724) names the Linux `PATH` step after `install.sh`.
- [accuknox/help#671](https://github.com/accuknox/help/pull/671) fixes a knoxctl page that named 0.9.0 while the installer fetched 0.9.58.

https://twitter.com/i/web/status/2108903653411021062

## Version 2 Finished More Runs at a Lower Cost

The same 4 targets ran twice. v2 added the planner fix, recovery and verify.

- Quickstarts that ended passed or verified went from 2 of 4 to 3 of 4.
- Failed steps recovered went from 0 to 3.
- Fixes proven in a fresh container went from 0 to 1.
- Cost per run, from neatlogs, went from $0.0262 to $0.0200.
- Time per run went from 128 s to 201 s.

v2 runs 73 seconds longer, because a verified fix runs the whole quickstart twice.

The sample is thin. Each target ran once per version, and several fixes landed together, so they share the credit.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109298807145984482

## The Business Plan Set the Agent's Spending Cap

Before the plan existed, the cap was a guess of $0.50 per run. Then `firstrun econ` read 88 run traces from neatlogs. The old cap sat at 30 times the mean run cost of $0.0178.

[cfo.ai](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE) modeled 18 months from those traces. Under the old cap, cash goes negative in month 14. At a 70% margin floor, the Scale tier cap comes out at $0.028 per run.

The executor now checks the tier cap in a `budget` span. A free-tier run on the typer quickstart stopped at step 4 with `cost budget spent: $0.0115 of $0.0108`.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109532415253160435

> **Rule of thumb:** Measure the cost per run first. Then derive the cap from your margin floor.

## The Agent Printed a Receipt, Then Held Back 13 Pages

A docs agent earns trust when it shows the bill for every run and declines work a repo's rules forbid.

**The homepage shows only real failures.** Each error on the FirstRun homepage, such as `entire: command not found`, came from a real run.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109275541471642063

**Every run ends with a bill.** The AccuKnox knoxctl run cost $0.0453 in model use, from 10,963 input and 1,941 output tokens. Compute added $0.0020, for $0.0473 in total. That is 96.4% of the Team cap and 162.5% of the Scale cap. At Scale prices the margin is 52.5%, under the 70% floor.

The receipt also hashes each evidence file, and `firstrun receipt --check` fails when one changed.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109290749392977988

**An audit costs less than one run.** Doc-audit reads a repo's git history to find stale docs pages. The first 7 audits cost $0.014609 together. dbt-core cost the most at $0.005498, for 7 Jev calls over 11,552 commits. All 7 figures are estimates from a re-run on 11 October.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109320952496439615

**The team map found the single owner.** On the AccuKnox help docs, 9 of 9 areas rest on one person. That person is me, with 425 commits. 8 of the top 10 tasks name me, and 2 have no clear owner.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109305809133793372

**The proof page lists its own gaps.** The For Judges page maps every claim to its file. It also says 38 of 113 non-merge commits carry no Entire checkpoint, and that two proof pages need a login.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109344819331862886

**The agent held back 13 pages.** FirstRun fixed and verified 16 docs pages. 3 of those pages became 4 PRs. Of the other 13, 10 needed only a container fix, so the docs were right. 3 had docs gaps.

- Flask runs `flask run` with no `--app`.
- Hypothesis gives an install line that skips pytest.
- HTTPX sets `r.encoding` after `r.text`.

The Pallets LLM policy, the Hypothesis AI policy and the HTTPX discussion-first rule ruled out an agent PR on all 3. So FirstRun opened 0 new PRs. I posted the HTTPX gap by hand as discussion #3801 on Saturday, and Polars issue #29855 the same day.

https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2109260603353079855

## I Would Not Build Two Cost Counters Again

FirstRun and neatlogs each count the cost of a run. On 43 matched runs, FirstRun counts 39% higher. The cap reads FirstRun's count, so it stops a run early and never late. That is safe, and it still gives two numbers for one fact. I will merge them into one counter next.

## Copy the Verify Rule Into Your Own Agent

1. Run the fix in a container that the fixing agent never touched.
2. Block every model call inside the check, and raise an error if one fires.
3. Add a test that fails if the check imports the planner or the fixer.
4. Mark a run verified only when every runnable step passes.
5. Report every other ending as not verified, and say why.

## Three Questions Get Short Answers

**Does FirstRun open a PR on its own?** No. It opens a docs PR only after the user says yes.

**What does one run cost?** The mean is $0.0178 over 88 runs, at list price.

**Can my own coding agent run it?** Yes. The site takes a docs URL and writes a prompt for your coding agent.

## Appendix

```bash
firstrun <url>
firstrun bisect <run> --package <pkg>
firstrun prereqs <run>
firstrun receipt RUN_ID --html
firstrun receipt --check runs/RUN_ID/receipt.json
```

- Site: https://firstrun.atharvashah.com
- Repo: https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun
- Demo video, 2:54: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9xxgu_1bH-E

content.content:
---
name: substack-writer
description: The Substack long-form writing harness. Use when drafting, developing, tightening, polishing, publishing or fixing a Substack blog article or long-form essay, including a post that is already live. It forces Atharva's opinion into the piece, runs every scorer to zero, then runs the polish pass (images, captions, embeds, diagrams, fact checks) and the publication QA that the 2026-09-26 audit of all 81 posts produced. Triggers on writing, drafting, improving, polishing or auditing a Substack post, blog article or long essay, on "make it 10/10", or on moving an idea toward a draft.
---

# Substack Writer

The goal is a sharp, opinionated piece that reads like a tired expert wrote a great second draft and scores zero on the slop (AI-shaped prose a scorer can measure) validator. Boring is a defect. So is genericism, so is an AI-tell.

Followers watch in an app. Subscribers are the owned list, the only asset that becomes a business. Notes get discovered, chat closes, and the article is where a reader decides you are worth paying for, so it has to prove something the free feed cannot. Write for the reader still around in two years. Every piece needs at least one line quotable with no context around it, because punchlines travel and paragraphs do not.

## A Short Prompt Still Gets the Whole Loop

"Write a post about X", "polish this" and "fix that live post" each mean every step below. Never
decide that a step is unnecessary because the post looks fine. Each failure the audit found
looked fine to the model that caused it. A post is done only when every line of this list is
true, and each line names the command that proves it:

| Done when | Proof |
|---|---|
| Slop CRIT is 0 | `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>" --write` |
| Clarity CRIT is 0 | Run `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py` with no arguments. It scans every file, and a file missing from its report has CRIT 0. A path argument is ignored today and prints "0 files", which checks nothing |
| Craft findings are 0 | `python SCRIPTS/substack/craft.py "<file>"` |
| Publication QA CRIT is 0, and each MED is fixed or named | `python SCRIPTS/substack/post_qa.py "<file>"` |
| Every image, figure and embed was opened and checked against its paragraph | [polish.md](references/polish.md) steps 2 to 4 |
| Every fact about a third party was checked against its source | [polish.md](references/polish.md) step 5 |
| A second reader found no contradiction | [polish.md](references/polish.md) step 9 |
| After publishing, the live post passes too | `python SCRIPTS/substack/post_qa.py "<file>" --live` and `sync_audit.py audit "<file>"` |

The rules for images, captions, embeds and diagrams are in `SUBSTACK/PUBLICATION STANDARD.md`.
The procedure is in [polish.md](references/polish.md). The writing gate hook runs `post_qa.py` on
every write to `2_PUBLISHED` and blocks on a CRIT.

**Read first:** `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md` (the bar every insight clears: non-obvious and tactical, box 4 only), `Digital Twin/Long-Form Writing Rules.md` (craft, the four beats, the headline), `Digital Twin/Voice.md` (persona), `Digital Twin/Audience.md` (who). Ban lists live in `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py`. This skill does not restate any of them.

## The loop (do not skip a step)

0. **Triage.** `python SCRIPTS/substack/overlap.py check "<the idea>"`. On `ABSORB` or `MERGE`, stop and propose folding it into the named article instead of drafting. The corpus is 79 published and 100 drafts, so the odds that a new idea is genuinely new are worse than they feel. Procedure and pushback script in `substack-idea-triage`. Only continue past this step on `WRITE` or a named `DIFFERENTIATE` angle, or on his explicit override.
1. **Intake.** Run [intake.md](references/intake.md). It forces the position: the hot take, the one story or number only Atharva has, the calm story, the plunge, who it is for, the goal. Answers fill the frontmatter intent fields. Skip only if he already supplied them. The friction is the point. Then write the headline claim as one sentence and name its box from `core/net-new-value.md`. The headline claim and every section claim must be box 4, or the piece is a summary of the field.
2. **Draft.** Against the craft rules, with [patterns.md](references/patterns.md) for how the best long-form writers build a piece, and [scannable.md](references/scannable.md) for the page shape: TL;DR, a before and after scenario, step headings, bullets, callouts, figures, FAQ, no table images. Lay the piece on the four beats (rule 8 of the rules file) before writing a paragraph. A draft that cannot name which beat each section serves has no arc yet.
3. **The 10% cut.** Cut a tenth of the words before touching any validator. Warm-up fluff up top, the middle sentence repeating a made point, the safe filler. This step only removes. Adding anything means the cut has not happened.
4. **Deterministic pass.** `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>" --write`. Fix every CRIT, re-run, iterate. Never argue with a CRIT.
4b. **Clarity pass.** `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py`, then find this file in the report. Today the scorer skips a path argument and prints "0 files", which looks clean and checks nothing. Take CRIT to 0. Every CRIT names a term coined in this vault, so the reader who searches for it gets somebody else's meaning. Gloss it where it first appears, or open the piece with a concepts table.
5. **Review passes.** A read-through for AI-tells the validator cannot see, then conviction and flow against [benchmarks.md](references/benchmarks.md), then optional `seo-blog-grader`.
6. **Headline last**, once the piece has a spine. Rules are the "The headline" section of the rules file, including its three-question check. Start each candidate from one of the twelve shapes in [titles.md](references/titles.md). Offer two candidates for Substack's A/B test: one promising a clear solution, one leading with the paradox. Make the pair differ by question (belief challenged, value given, emotion triggered), never by wording alone. On the publish screen, click "continue", toggle on "run a test title", toggle on "include subtitles", and test two titles with two subtitles. Keep Substack's recommended size, which is one hour on 40% of readers. The title updates to the winner on its own and a results email follows.
6b. **Paid-tier proposal.** Atharva runs a paid tier. Never decide on your own that a piece is paid or free, and never place a paywall break yourself. Propose the split and wait for his answer. The proposal names which piece is free or paid, where the break goes, and the one pain point the paid part solves.

   Follow Hook, Trust, Value, Upgrade. Put the hook, the proof and one useful result above the break, and the full system below it. Check that every free paragraph backs the headline promise. Source: [Substack Tips - Liz Leatrice](../../../LIBRARY/Notes/Substack%20Tips%20-%20Liz%20Leatrice.md).
7. **Craft gate.** `python SCRIPTS/substack/craft.py "<file>"`, get it to 0. Reports only, never edits.
7b. **Polish pass.** Run [polish.md](references/polish.md) from step 1 to step 9, in order. It
   gives every image one home and a real caption, adds embeds that prove a claim, draws each
   process or comparison in the diagram engine, checks every fact about a third party, and ends
   with a second reader. Its first and last command is `python SCRIPTS/substack/post_qa.py "<file>"`,
   which must reach CRIT 0.
8. **Stamp.** `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>" --write` and `python SCRIPTS/seo/score.py "<file>" --write`.
9. **Publish, then check the live post.** Publishing needs Atharva's explicit word
   (`substack-cli` skill). After the post is live, run
   `python SCRIPTS/substack/post_qa.py "<file>" --live`. Fix a live problem with
   `SCRIPTS/substack/live_edit.py`, never with a full `update`, then mirror the fix into the vault
   and run `python SCRIPTS/substack/sync_audit.py audit "<file>"`. [polish.md](references/polish.md)
   step 8 explains why.
10. **Announce.** Render the load-order (the sequence rule files load in) panel with `python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill substack-writer --file "<path>" --node "<node>" --topic "<the idea>"`. It looks the chain up itself and runs every scorer that applies, so the checks half is measured rather than typed.

## Shape of the piece

**800 to 2,000 words, 1,800 the sweet spot.** Density is the metric, so if `target_length` fights the idea, say so and write the honest length. There is deliberately no minimum in the craft gate.

**One saveable block per tactical piece.** A box 4 piece carries one dense block a reader copies and keeps: a numbered rule, a short table or a command. Label it by what it does, such as "The verify rule". Place it in the last third, before the closer, and keep it under 120 words. An argument piece with no step to copy has none, and a checklist stapled to the end of an argument deflates it (see [patterns.md](references/patterns.md)). Source: the "screenshot-worthy section" in [Alex Prompter's X Article prompt](https://x.com/alex_prompter/status/2025884386001138056). Its emoji cap, cliffhanger closer and "impossible claim" headline conflict with `Voice.md` and the fabrication rule, so skip them.

**Hand off to the flywheel (one piece of work that feeds the next).** A finished essay already contains its three Notes, so name them in the handoff instead of making `substack-notes` invent content later. Awareness is the opening story, education is the core rule from the middle, conviction is the belief that made him write it.

## The two scorers

| | `slop/score.py` | `substack/craft.py` |
|---|---|---|
| Sees | Prose: banned words, punctuation, flow | Structure: headline, pacing, arc |
| Score | `10*CRIT + 3*MED + 1*LOW` | Weighted findings, 0 = clean |
| Gate | Pre-commit blocks `2_PUBLISHED` on CRIT > 0 | Advisory in pre-commit |

**slop CRIT** (10): em-dash, en-dash, semicolon, hard banned word, AI-tell phrase, corrective antithesis. **MED** (3): soft words and phrases, monotone or long sentences, heavy passive. **LOW** (1): adverb and hedge density, tricolons, long paragraphs, repeated openers. It skips code, tables, quotes, and URLs.

**craft findings:** `headline-no-keyword` and `headline-keyword-thin` mean the headline lost its keywords. `headline-topic-shaped` means it names a subject instead of an outcome. `headline-colon` wants a period. `headline-no-number` is advisory. `wall-of-text` is a paragraph past 4 sentences and 70 words. `robot-spacing` is every sentence on its own line. `warmup-intro` is a self-explaining opener. `over-band` is past 2,000 words, and does not apply to `2_PUBLISHED`.

Tune ban lists in `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py`, then `python SCRIPTS/slop/rules_prompt.py --write` to resync `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

## Frontmatter

`type` runs `Idea` -> `Draft Article` -> `Article`. Never write the deprecated `publish_date`, `social_flywheel`, `internal_links`, `title`, `subtitle`, or `description`. Full schema in `SUBSTACK/README.md`.

```yaml
---
type: Draft Article
seo_title: ""           # THE headline. <= 60 chars, hard max
seo_description: ""     # THE dek. 80-160 chars
created: 2026-07-22
updated: 2026-07-22
url_slug: ""            # <= 60 chars, power words, no stopwords
category: ""            # Tech and AI | Biz and Growth | Money and Career | Entertainment and Culture
cover: ""               # ../_COVERS/<url_slug>-cover.png
planned_date:           # informational only
goal: ""                # subscribers, authority, leads
target_keywords: []     # primary first, its content words must appear in seo_title
target_audience: ""     # which ICP from Audience.md
core_message: ""        # the one sentence a reader repeats afterward
target_length: ""
ai_slop_score:          # 0 = clean
seo_score:              # 0 = clean
---
```

Each `seo_*` field publishes twice: `seo_title` is both the visible headline and Google's `<title>`, `seo_description` is both the dek and the meta description. That is why 60 characters is a hard ceiling, not an ideal.

**The body is the article and nothing else.** After the closing `---` comes the first sentence or first heading. Never emit a cover embed, a `#substack` tag, `**Source:**`/`**Article:**`/`**Source Batch Title:**`/`**Social Assets:**` scaffolding, a frontmatter restatement, or an `# H1` repeating the title. No internal links, no `internal_links` field.

## Fixing a Post That Is Already Live

Skip steps 0 to 3. Run steps 4 to 9 on the vault file in `2_PUBLISHED`, and edit the live post
with `live_edit.py` as [polish.md](references/polish.md) step 8 describes. Keep his voice. Fix
what is wrong and leave what is working, because every change to a live post is a risk.

## When an idea or draft is dropped in

Run intake first. Skip only when he has already stated goal, audience, and core message. Never invent an opinion for him. Pull it out, then write it sharp.

# Polish Pass: Images, Embeds, Diagrams and Facts

This file is the procedure that takes a clean draft to a 10/10 post. The rules live in
`SUBSTACK/PUBLICATION STANDARD.md`. This file says how to meet them, step by step, with the
command that proves each step. Every step came from the 2026-09-26 audit of all 81 published
posts, which found the failures listed in section 7 by hand.

Do the steps in order. Do not skip a step because the post "looks fine". Each failure in
section 7 looked fine to the model that caused it.

## 1. Run the Checker First to See What Is Broken

```bash
python SCRIPTS/substack/post_qa.py "<article.md>"
```

Read every line. CRIT must reach 0 on the vault file before the post ships, and again on the live post after it ships. A clean live post does not excuse a dirty vault file, because the next `update` pushes the vault file. MED lines are real defects too, so fix
each one unless the fix would make the post worse, and say which ones you left and why. A LOW
`embed-gap` line is a hint, never a quota.

## 2. Give Every Image One Home and One Honest Caption

1. Read the paragraph above each image. The image must show what that paragraph talks about.
   If it does not, move the image line to the paragraph that does.
2. Look at the image itself with the Read tool. Never caption an image you did not open.
3. Write the caption as the alt text, `![caption](path)`. One sentence, 20 words or fewer.
   - A screenshot: name the tool or view, and the detail to notice.
   - A diagram or chart: state its takeaway, never its topic.
   - A still, cover or poster: name the work, the studio and the year.
   - A table image: no caption.
4. The same picture never appears twice. `post_qa.py` compares pixels, so a renamed copy is caught.
5. Download any outside image into `META/Attachments/<url_slug>/`. A hotlink dies.

## 3. Add Embeds That Prove a Claim

An embed is an X post, a YouTube video or a Substack post card. The tier table in the standard
sets the range by length. Stop below the range when the material is weak.

### 3a. Find Candidates in This Order

1. Atharva's own X posts (`x.com/cultist_dev`). One per article at most, and only when the post
   says the same thing the paragraph says.
2. Accounts he follows. Pull them with `x.py` inside WSL, or through the Composio MCP when WSL
   fails. The recipe is in the memory note `reference_x_api_via_composio_mcp`.
3. First-party sources: the tool's own channel, the author, the studio, the official trailer.
4. Other credible voices, such as a known practitioner or a publication.

Search tools that work on this machine:

```bash
yt-dlp --flat-playlist --print "%(id)s | %(title)s | %(channel)s | %(duration)s" "ytsearch8:<query>"
python "D:\Atharva\NOTES\SCRIPTS\keys\keys.py" firecrawl
```

The second command prints a Firecrawl key for web search. Reddit works only through Apify.

### 3b. Verify Each Candidate Before You Use It

1. **The URL is real.** Never type a URL from memory. Every embed URL comes from a search result
   or an API response you saw in this session.
2. **A video shows the scene the paragraph describes.** Read the title and the channel. Then
   fetch three frames and look at them:

   ```bash
   curl -s -o f1.jpg "https://i.ytimg.com/vi/<id>/1.jpg"
   ```

   Frames `1.jpg`, `2.jpg` and `3.jpg` sit at 25, 50 and 75 percent of the clip. The audit swapped
   three film clips that showed a different scene from the one the text analysed.
3. **An X post agrees with the article.** Read its full text. Cut any post that makes a claim the
   article does not support, such as a number or a timeline the article never states.
4. **The embed is new to the corpus.** `post_qa.py` flags a URL another published post uses.
5. **The embed hydrates.** A `live_edit.py` dry run fetches each one from Substack and fails on a
   fake URL.

### 3c. Place Each Embed

1. Write one lead-in sentence of 20 words or fewer. It names the speaker, or what the clip shows.
2. Put the marker on its own line directly after that lead-in paragraph:

   ```markdown
   Andrej Karpathy builds a tokenizer from scratch in this lecture.

   <!-- substack youtube2 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zduSFxRajkE -->
   ```

   Types are `youtube2`, `twitter2` and `embeddedPost`.
3. Never put two embeds in a row, and never put one below the **Related reading** line.
4. When you delete an embed, delete its lead-in too. The audit found a lead-in that introduced
   a removed post.

## 4. Draw Diagrams in the Diagram Engine

Draw a figure when a section explains a process, a comparison, a stack, a cycle, a before and
after, or an architecture. Never redraw a screenshot, a photo or a film still. Never use an
image model.

1. Pick the closest existing figure in `SUBSTACK/_DIAGRAM-ENGINE/figures/`. Copy it to
   `figures/<url_slug>-<name>.html`.
2. Write the title first. It states the claim, the same claim the paragraph makes.
3. Build each box from a sentence in the post. A box that no sentence supports is a fabrication.
   Keep to about 50 words of box text, 7 nodes in a flow and one yellow accent.
4. Render it, and fix the file until the render prints no `LINT` line:

   ```bash
   python SUBSTACK/_DIAGRAM-ENGINE/render.py figures/<url_slug>-<name>.html
   ```

5. Open `out/<url_slug>-<name>.png` with the Read tool and read every label.
6. Copy it to `META/Attachments/<url_slug>/fig-<url_slug>-<name>.png`, and give it an alt text
   that states the takeaway.
7. Compare the figure with the text one last time. The audit re-drew 9 figures whose titles or
   boxes said something the post did not, such as a one-time fee the post never mentioned.

The class names and the nine rules are in `SUBSTACK/_DIAGRAM-ENGINE/README.md`.

## 5. Check Every Fact About Someone Else

Check each claim about a third party against its source before the post ships. That covers a
product's price or pricing model, a date, a count, a sequence of books or albums, and the
spelling of a name. The audit fixed a paid tool described as a one-time fee, a book order that
was backwards, "ten years" that was three, a percentage off by a factor of ten, and a
misspelled company name. When a claim cannot be checked, cut it or say where it came from.

## 6. Make the Structure Clean for Substack

1. No H1 in the body, because the title is already the H1. Change a stray H1 to `##`. The one exception is a long post split into parts, where an H1 may open each part.
2. Put a book, film, album or game title in italics, `*The Graduate*`, in headings and prose.
3. Keep an image out of a numbered list, because Substack restarts the numbering at 1 after it.
4. Fence every code block with a language. An unfenced `/**` comment split one code block into
   six pieces.
5. Keep links out of table cells. A table publishes as an image, and a link renders as raw text.
6. Gloss each owned or niche term where it first appears. `SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py` finds them.

## 7. The Failures the Audit Found, and What Now Stops Each One

| Failure found on 2026-09-26 | Count | What stops it now |
|---|---|---|
| The same image twice in one post | 38 | `post_qa.py` dup-image, by path, caption and pixels |
| A caption that repeats a heading or says "image 2" | 159 | `post_qa.py` caption checks, and step 2 above |
| An embed pushed below the closing links | 13 blocks | The anchor rule in section 8, and `post_qa.py` after-related |
| A hotlinked image that died | 2 | `post_qa.py` hotlink |
| A clip showing a different scene | 3 | Step 3b, the frame check |
| An X post off topic or against the article | 5 removed | Step 3b, read the full post |
| A figure that says what the text does not | 9 | Step 4, one box per sentence |
| A wrong fact about a third party | 6 posts | Step 5 |
| An old title left as a body H1 | 4 | `post_qa.py` h1-in-body |
| A list restarting at 1 after an image | 30 lists | `post_qa.py` image-in-list, and `live_edit.py` list_start |
| Literal asterisks or a raw link in the live post | 2 | `post_qa.py --live` md-leak, and step 6 |

## 8. Edit a Live Post Without Breaking It

A published post changes through one of two tools. Pick by the size of the change.

- **A small fix** (a caption, a moved image, one sentence, an embed, a removed block): use
  `SCRIPTS/substack/live_edit.py`. It edits the live post node by node, backs it up, and
  confirms that the date, slug, title and email state did not move. Dry run first, then `--live`.
- **A rewrite:** use `substack.py update`. It rebuilds the whole body from the markdown.

`update` puts each embed back after the paragraph whose first 60 characters match the paragraph
it followed before. If you reword the start of that paragraph, the embed falls to the end of the
post. So on a published post, never reword the first 60 characters of a paragraph that sits
directly above an embed marker, or use `live_edit.py` for that change.

After any live change:

1. Make the same change in the vault file.
2. Run both checks:

   ```bash
   python SCRIPTS/substack/sync_audit.py audit "<article.md>"
   python SCRIPTS/substack/post_qa.py "<article.md>" --live
   ```

   The first must print 0 posts needing attention. The second must show CRIT 0.

## 9. Get a Second Reader Before You Call It Done

The model that wrote the post cannot see its own contradictions. When subagents are available,
send one this brief: read the post, open every image and figure, read every embed's title or
text, and list each place where a caption, figure, embed or fact disagrees with the prose. Fix
what it finds. With no subagent, do the same pass yourself one item at a time, and write each
check down as you go.
# Scannable, Visual Articles

Use this file at step 2 (draft) and step 7b (polish). A reader scans the page before they decide to read it. The page must pay on the scan: the headings, the bullets, the callouts and the figures alone tell the story. Atharva set these rules on 2026-10-12 after a review of 7 refreshed posts.

## Shape the Page in Ten Parts

1. **TL;DR at the top.** After the first paragraph, give 3 to 5 bullets, each a full claim the reader keeps.
2. **One scenario that shows the payoff.** Put a before and after near the top: the same task without the idea and with it. Draw it as a figure, then tell it in 4 to 6 lines. Show the reader the result instead of telling them it matters.
3. **Steps as H2s.** In a how-to, each phase is an H2 that starts with "Step 1.", "Step 2." and so on, then names the action. A listicle uses "App 1.", "Tool 1." the same way.
4. **High level first, detail later.** Open with the whole system in one picture. Then go phase by phase into each part. Never alternate overview and detail.
5. **Bullets over paragraphs.** Any paragraph that names 3 or more items becomes a list. Keep a paragraph to 3 sentences. Put a blank line between every beat.
6. **Callouts for the lines worth saving.** A callout is a blockquote that opens with a bold label: Tip, Watch out, Example, Rule of thumb. Use 2 to 4 per post, never two in a row.
7. **Figures for every concept with parts.** A glossary is a network graph with the main idea in the center. A stack is a layer diagram. A process is a flow. A comparison is a before and after. Build each one in `SUBSTACK/_DIAGRAM-ENGINE`. Aim for one figure per 400 words.
8. **FAQ before the close.** Give 3 to 5 questions a newcomer asks, each answered in 2 or 3 sentences.
9. **Code goes to an appendix.** Scripts, config paths and long commands sit in a final "Appendix" section. The body explains the approach and the reason.
10. **Proof from his own products.** When the piece discusses something Atharva sells or gives away, link and screenshot it from atharvashah.com/tools or atharvashah.com/skill-pack. Capture the product's own page, never its grid card, at 16:9 (a 1600x900 viewport at 2x), with the cookie banner and chat bubble hidden. A /tools item gets its section heading at the top of the frame and a purple inset outline on its card. Put the link on the product name in the sentence, never around the image, because `substack.py` publishes a linked image `[![alt](src)](url)` as raw text.

## Never Ship These Five Things

1. A markdown table. Substack renders it as a flat image of a table. Turn it into a figure or a list.
2. A third-party photo of a person, or an embed card whose main visual is someone else's face or brand.
3. Commentary about an older version of the post, such as "In May this article named three tools". A refreshed post reads as the only version that ever existed.
4. Details from inside the vault: private paths, internal script names, incidental counts. A stranger must follow every line.
5. A closing run of paragraphs that summarize, reflect or inspire. End on the last useful thing, then the FAQ.

## Check the Scan Before Publishing

Read only the headings, the bold labels, the bullets and the figure titles. If that pass does not teach the main idea, the page is not finished.
