---
type: Identity Profile
title: "Pattern Rules"
description: "The AI failure shapes a regex cannot catch, and the human signals to protect."
created: 2026-08-22
updated: 2026-08-22
---

# Pattern Rules

> **Purpose:** `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` catches words. This file catches shapes. A draft can
> score CRIT 0 and still read like a machine wrote it, because the tell is the sentence structure
> and not the vocabulary. Loaded on every writing job, right after the runtime contract.
>
> Sections 1 to 4 say what to remove. Section 5 says what to leave alone, and it carries the same
> weight. Adapted from `core/anti-ai-rules.md` and `core/ai_slop_commandments.md` in
> [Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer](https://github.com/Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer). The mechanism notes are
> theirs. The wording and the thresholds are mine.

Each rule below names the pattern, the mechanism that produces it, and the fix. The mechanism
matters. A rule you understand survives a rewrite, and a rule you memorised does not.

## 1. Sentence shapes

**The copula dodge.** A model replaces `is` with `serves as`, `stands as`, `represents`, `marks`,
`boasts`, `features` or `offers`. The mechanism is a repetition penalty. The model avoids reusing
the common word `is`, and the substitute implies a relationship that does not exist. Write `is`.
Keep `serves as` only where a real function sits beyond plain identity.

**Tacked-on analysis.** A participle clause bolted to the end of a sentence to fake depth. The
shapes are `highlighting its importance`, `underscoring the shift`, `reflecting a broader trend`
and `marking a significant moment`. These clauses carry no new fact. They claim the fact before
them matters and supply no evidence. Cut the clause. If the significance is real, write it as its
own sentence with its own proof.

**Unearned significance.** A claim of impact, legacy or scale with no support in the same
paragraph. Watch for `a pivotal moment`, `a key turning point`, `setting the stage for` and
`an enduring legacy`. Training data rewards important-sounding prose, so the
model asserts importance and expects the evidence to arrive later. State only what the evidence
carries. Real significance falls out of the evidence on its own.

**The courtroom noun.** A judgment word standing in for a result nobody adjudicated. `verdict` is the
current one, and it arrives as `so the honest answer is not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation`
or as `the verdict is still out`. The same move hides in `ruling`, `the jury is out`, `case closed`,
`indictment` and `exonerates`. Two things break at once. The noun is a metaphor doing the work of a
number, and the `not a verdict, it's Y` frame negates a word the reader never proposed, which is the
banned antithesis with a straw man inside it. Write the result, the number, or the reason you cannot
tell yet. Keep the word where a real decision with named values exists, such as a court, or software
that emits one.

**Vague authority.** A claim attributed to an unnamed group. `Experts agree`, `studies suggest`,
`research shows`, `observers note` and `industry reports indicate` all simulate a source. Name the
expert, link the study, or drop the claim. There is no third option.

**The false range.** A `from X to Y` span where X and Y do not sit on one spectrum. The sentence
`From innovation to cultural change, AI is rewriting everything` reads as coverage and states
nothing. Name the two or three real things.

**Name-dropping.** A list of outlets, tools or names with no fact attached. `Featured in Forbes,
TechCrunch and Wired` names sources and says nothing. The model lists authority to borrow it. Pick
one name and say what it said, or cut the list.

**Abstract metaphor nouns.** A concrete idea dressed as a technical term. The set is `substrate`,
`vector` used for a way, `locus`, `vantage`, `nexus`, `bedrock`, `modality` and `endgame`. Each one
reads as precise and hides a plainer word: `base`, `way`, `place`, `last phase`. Pick the plain
word. His own working terms are exempt, because he chose them on purpose. `harness`, `flywheel`,
`scaffolding`, `surface` and `primitive` stay. The precedence ladder in the runtime contract
settles any other case, and it favours his voice.

**The aphorism formula.** An ordinary claim dressed as reusable wisdom. The shapes are
`X is the currency of Y`, `the architecture of X` and `X becomes a trap`. This sounds
profound and loses the fact. Rule 23 in `slop_rules.py` bans the clever one-liner. This is the
same failure with a formula behind it, so replace the formula with the concrete claim under it.

**The theatrical opener.** A standalone `Honestly?`, `Look,`, `Real talk` or `Here is the thing`
placed before an ordinary point. The tell is the fake reveal, because a person being honest just
says the thing. The same words mid-sentence in casual prose are ordinary English, so read the
position and not the word.

**Adverbs propping up weak verbs.** `He ran very quickly` hides `he sprinted`. When the adverb is
load-bearing, the verb is wrong. Replace the verb and delete the adverb.

**Elegant variation.** The model renames its subject to avoid repeating it, so one person becomes
`the researcher`, then `the prominent figure`, then `the key player`. Rule 28 says one word for one
thing. This is the mechanism it defends against. Repeat the real name.

## 2. Paragraph and section shapes

**False balance.** The three-step formula runs positive framing, then a nod at problems, then
instant dismissal. `Despite these challenges, the opportunity is enormous` is the shape of
analysis with none of the work. Engage the problem and let it stand, or drop the pretence.

**Tricolon saturation.** The rule of three is a real device and a model reaches for it by default,
because three items look thorough with no need to be thorough. One tricolon per paragraph, never
two in a row. Four real items get listed as four. Two real items get written as prose.

**The outline wrapper.** Section titles that a template chose rather than the content. The set is
`Challenges and future directions`, `Key takeaways`, `Legacy and impact`, `Overview` and
`Background`. Each one announces generation before a reader reads a word. Rule 4 in `Voice.md`
already demands a heading that states a conclusion, so name what the section delivers.

**Fractal recapping.** A summary before a section starts, and another after it ends. Both
`In this section we will cover` and `as we have seen` are padding inherited from textbooks. Rule 15
bans the trailing summary, and this rule bans the leading one. Write forward.

**Diff-anchored writing.** Prose that narrates a change instead of describing the thing. The line
`This section replaces the old onboarding flow` only makes sense to a reader who saw the old one. A
changelog, a release note and a migration guide are version-scoped by nature and are exempt.
Everything else reads coherently to a reader who arrived today.

**One-point dilution.** The same claim restated ten times across four thousand words, sold as depth.
Say the claim once. Then spend the length on evidence, on the counterargument, and on what follows.

**The undone claim.** A later line quietly reverses an earlier one. The hook promises a result and the
close hedges it. A post says "about thirty minutes" and its pinned comment says "under one hour". Each
line reads fine alone, so the writer is the least likely person to see it. Read line 1 against line 2,
line 2 against the body, the ending against the opening, and the pinned comment against the post. Fix
the weaker line and leave the stronger one. Never rewrite both.

**The echo stack.** Three or more consecutive lines built on one skeleton, such as "The page lacks X.
There is no Y. Z does not exist." The model repeats the last structure it wrote, and a person
escalates. Make each line add a fact or raise the cost, keep the strongest, and put the rest in one
list whose items differ in shape. Swapping synonyms into the same skeleton keeps the echo.

## 3. Fill that is not content

**Assistant bleed.** The set is `I hope this helps`, `Certainly`, `Would you like me to`,
`Feel free to adjust` and `Here is a draft of`. Each one belongs in a chat window, and inside a
deliverable each one is contamination. Start with the content.

**Cutoff disclaimers.** The set is `As of my last update`, `while specific details are limited`
and `based on available information`. Each one is a hedge formatted as content. Say the honest
thing once instead, or ask him.

**Placeholder leakage.** An unfilled field that ships. `[insert link]`, `INSERT_SOURCE_URL`,
`access-date 2026-XX-XX` and `add image if available` all reach the reader when nobody re-read the
draft. A bracket from the fabrication rule is deliberate and stays visible on purpose. A bracket
from a template is a defect.

**Promotional register.** The set is `nestled`, `in the heart of`, `vibrant`, `boasts`, `renowned`
and `a diverse array`. All of it comes from tourism copy and press releases. Write the neutral
declarative version instead.
Rule 8 in `Voice.md` says the same thing from the other side, so say what the thing does.

## 4. Formatting tells

**Em dash density.** Already CRIT in `slop_rules.py`, so this is the reason behind that ban. Model
output uses the em dash far above human rates and puts it where a comma belongs. Do not trade the em
dash for parentheses or an en dash. That move swaps one tell for another. End the sentence, or use a
comma.

**The colon as a connector.** A colon that joins two clauses mid-sentence fakes a cause. The line
`The fix is simple: you rewrite the query` adds nothing that a period would not. A colon is correct
before a list or an example. Everywhere else, end the sentence. Rule 17 in `slop_rules.py` already
bans a colon in a heading, and this is the same tell inside a line.

**Bold on every key phrase in running prose.** Emphasis stops meaning anything once it is
everywhere. Reserve bold for a term you are defining, or for a label that opens a line. Rule 2 in
`Voice.md` sets the boundary per folder. A bold label must earn its place with a new fact after it.
`**Performance:** Performance improved 40%` fails, because the label only repeats the line.
`**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file` passes, because the detail is new.

**Sentence case in an H2.** Every H2 uses AP Title Case, in every channel, and states the claim
its section proves. `SCRIPTS/slop/heading_case.py` blocks a miscased H2 and flags a topic label.
H1 and H3 and below keep the case their destination uses. A model that capitalises every word of
an H3 or a body label is still showing the old tell.

**A skipped heading level, or a rule above every heading.** Jumping H2 to H4, or dropping `---`
before each section by reflex, are both template tics. Neither is a writing choice.

## 5. What to leave alone

Sections 1 to 4 are a list of things to remove. Applied without judgement they produce the second
failure, which is prose stripped so hard that nobody is home. That output is not human. It is a
different machine's output, and it is the source of every complaint that edited writing reads flat,
boring and sanded down.

**None of the following is evidence of AI on its own.** Do not cut one unless it sits in a cluster
with real tells.

- Clean grammar and a consistent style. Many writers are edited. Polish proves nothing.
- Formal vocabulary. The banned list names specific overused words. It does not ban intelligence.
  Leave "ostensibly", "notwithstanding" and "constituent" where they are the right word.
- A mix of casual and formal register. That usually marks a technical writer, not a chatbot.
- Dry, plain prose. For a runbook it is correct.
- One transition word. A single "however" is English. The pile-up is the tell.
- One short emphatic sentence. People land points with a clipped sentence. Flag the drumbeat only
  when several stack up and inflate the tone.
- A salutation or a sign-off. Letters are older than chatbots.
- An unsourced claim. Most writing is unsourced. That is a rigor problem and not an AI problem.
- A watched word inside a quotation, a title, a proper noun or an example. When the piece discusses
  the phrase rather than uses it, leave it exactly as written.

## 6. What to protect

Removing tells is half the job. The other half is leaving alive whatever was already alive. These
are the hardest things for a model to produce and the easiest for an eager edit to erase.

- **Odd, specific, hard-to-invent detail.** A real address. A strange quote. "The lawyer who worked
  upstairs from my dentist." Models round specifics off and people hoard them. Never generalise one
  of these to make a sentence flow.
- **Mixed feelings left unresolved.** "I think this is mostly right and it still bothers me." A
  model defaults to a clean take. Do not resolve the tension for him.
- **Dated references.** Slang, a meme, an in-joke anchored to one year and one subculture. Models
  lag by a year, so these are strong human signal.
- **A genuine aside or a self-correction.** A parenthesis where the writer interrupts himself.
  Machines rarely do that.
- **Uneven rhythm.** A nine-word sentence next to a forty-word one. Model output drifts toward one
  uniform mid-length cadence. The variance is the signal, so never regularise it.
- **An opinion he can defend.** If he can say why he chose a word, that reasoning outranks every
  rule in this file.
- **A deliberate quirk.** A writer who always opens lowercase, or never uses a semicolon, is doing
  something. Match it.

**The operating principle is clusters, not instances.** One em dash means nothing. An em dash plus
a tricolon plus "vibrant tapestry" plus a "Challenges" heading is a confession.

When you cannot tell whether something is his voice or a machine default, the precedence ladder in
the runtime contract decides it. Assume it is his, and leave it.

**When a draft carries none of the signals in section 6, the problem is not that AI patterns
remain.** The problem is that nobody is home. Adding a specific, a stance and some unevenness beats
deleting one more banned word. The fabrication rule sets the limit on how a specific gets added.
It comes from him, never from invention.

## 7. The pass before you hand it over

Run this after the scorer reaches CRIT 0, because the scorer cannot see any of it.

- [ ] Any "serves as" or "represents a" standing in for "is"?
- [ ] Any tacked-on participle claiming significance?
- [ ] Any impact claim with no evidence beside it?
- [ ] Any unnamed authority carrying a fact?
- [ ] Two tricolons in a row, or a tricolon that hides four real items?
- [ ] A template heading, a leading recap, or a trailing recap?
- [ ] Any assistant bleed, cutoff hedge or leftover placeholder?
- [ ] Any colon joining two clauses where a period belongs?
- [ ] Any bold label that only repeats the line after it?
- [ ] Any metaphor noun where a plain word fits, outside his working terms?
- [ ] Any list of names or outlets with no fact attached?
- [ ] Any fact, name, number or source that he did not supply?
- [ ] Does any later line undo an earlier one? Read the hook against line 2, the body against the pinned comment, and the ending against the opening.
- [ ] Cover everything after the opening. Can you still guess how the piece ends? If so, the hook answered itself.
- [ ] Did anything from section 5 get cut that should have stayed?
- [ ] Did every signal in section 6 survive the edit?
- [ ] List every heading in the draft on one line. Does any heading state an outline slot rather than a claim, so it would sit unchanged over a different topic?
- [ ] Find the one sentence in the draft that only Atharva could have written: a real date, a named person, a number from his own work, a moment he was wrong. If no such sentence exists, the draft is not done.
- [ ] If the piece covers several parallel items, read only the closing line of each one in a row. Do they all sound interchangeable with the nouns swapped?

## 7b. Fixing a MED without creating the next one

Each advisory the scorer raises has one right fix. The other fix costs four to six rounds of
edit-and-rescore, and that is where most of the time on a clean draft goes.

**`readability-fragment` and `readability-bullet-fragment`: add a finite verb, never merge.**
"Speed multiplier." becomes "A speed multiplier finishes their own tasks faster." Do not fold
the fragment into the sentence before it. Measured across `2_PUBLISHED` and `1_DRAFTS` on
2026-08-29: adding a verb created a new `ste-long-sentence` hit in 0 of 239 paragraphs, and
merging created one in 6. A fragment caps at nine words and a long sentence starts at
twenty-one, so a verb cannot cross the gap. A merge can.

**`repeated-consecutive-opener`: escalate, do not reword.** Three lines that open on the same word
are an echo stack (section 2). Keep the strongest line, make each other line add a fact or raise the
cost, or fold the weak ones into one list whose items differ in shape.

**`ste-long-sentence`: split at the clause, and check the halves.** Halving a 45-word
sentence leaves two 22-word sentences, both still over. Cut to the real clause boundary
instead, or drop a subordinate clause outright.

**`ste-progressive` and `ste-perfect`: change the tense, do not restructure.** "They were
publishing videos" becomes "They published videos". A rewrite around the verb pulls a
fragment or a long sentence in behind it.

**`readability-long-paragraph`: cut a sentence, do not join two.** Joining two sentences to
lower the count is the move that produces a long sentence. The scorer now only raises this
when the paragraph still holds a sentence over 20 words, so splitting one is always safe.

## 8. Corpus-level shapes

Sections 1 to 4 catch a tell inside one sentence or one paragraph. These four hide at the
scale of the whole piece, or across many pieces, so a single-file read misses them. The 2026-08-28
audit of all 78 published articles found each one repeating across most of the corpus, on
unrelated topics, which is what told a reader the pattern was the machine and not the writer.
Full findings: [AI Slop Reader Audit, 2026-08-28](../../INBOX/Reports/AI-Slop-Reader-Audit-2026-08-28.md).

**The generic macro-skeleton.** Hook, why-it-matters, a numbered list or a run of parallel
sections, a recap, a closing call to action. A reader who has read enough AI explainers
recognizes this shape before evaluating a single claim in it, because the same headings
("Why This Matters", "Key Takeaways", "The Bigger Takeaway", "Wrapping Up", "Who This Is For")
would sit unchanged over almost any other topic. A heading must name the specific claim inside
its section, not the outline slot it fills. Found in roughly 83% of the audited corpus.

**Zero first-person specificity.** Strip the byline and the piece runs unchanged on any other
blog covering the same topic, because every example is a generic hypothetical "you" or an
unnamed archetype rather than a named person, a real date, a real number from his own work, or
a moment he was wrong or surprised. This is the concrete thing a "reads AI" complaint detects,
even when the reader cannot name a rule. Every piece needs at least one detail only Atharva
could supply, woven into the opening or the close, not bolted on as an afterthought paragraph.
Found in roughly 64% of the audited corpus, the single most common reason cited.

**Per-item template stamping.** When a piece covers several parallel items (tools, films,
terms, chapters, entries in a series), every item runs through the identical clause-by-clause
mold: same heading shape, same bolded lead-in, same closing "lesson" sentence. A reader can
predict item 4 after reading item 2, which reads as one template with new nouns dropped in
rather than several separate acts of thinking. Vary structure across items on purpose: let
length, opening move, and closing move differ per entry so no two are interchangeable with the
nouns swapped. Concentrated in, but not limited to, multi-part series (Film School in Scenes,
Slaying Your 20s, the Uketsu deep dives) and long enumerations (a glossary, a tool roundup).

**Announcing significance instead of demonstrating it.** Stock transition phrases that promise
weight the next sentence has not earned yet: "Here's the thing", "Here is what matters", "Let
me explain", "Here's the part most people miss". Stacking two or three of these in one short
piece reads as connective filler standing in for an actual transition. Delete the announcing
sentence and let the next sentence open the paragraph directly. If the paragraph reads weaker
without the announcement, the claim itself is not strong enough yet, so rewrite the claim
rather than propping it up with a preamble.

A fifth shape from the same audit is not new prose to avoid, it is a gap in the mechanical
scorer: "X is not Y. It is Z." across two full sentences performs the exact negate-then-reveal
move that `ANTITHESIS_PATTERNS` in `slop_rules.py` already bans when it is joined by a comma,
and slips past untouched because the scorer checks one sentence at a time. Treat it as banned
under the same rule until the detector is extended to match across a sentence boundary.

## 9. The Wikipedia cross-check, 2026-08-28

Atharva ran [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing)
plus a companion 38-badge detector list against this file. Most of the 38 were already covered by
a rule above under different wording (not-only-but-also, it's-important-to-note, testament,
crucial role, the ever-evolving landscape, the challenges-and-outlook formula, the tacked-on
participle, promotional boilerplate, chatbot leftovers). The genuine gaps are now mechanically
enforced in `slop_rules.py` and `score.py` rather than restated here, see `TIC_PATTERNS`,
`HARD_PHRASES`, and the stacked-questions and echoing-sentences checks in `score.py` for the
mechanism and the exact strings. Do not copy that list into this file, it would drift.

A second pass on the same day built a probe file with one example sentence per badge and ran the
scorer over it. That probe found 20 of the 38 still silent, so the first pass had missed more than
it claimed. The 20 landed as 9 new regex shapes in `TIC_PATTERNS`, 4 advisory shapes in the new
`TIC_PATTERNS_SOFT`, a `repeated-consecutive-opener` run check in `score.py`, and about 50 new
fixed strings in `HARD_PHRASES` and `SOFT_PHRASES`. A backtest over 607 files across the vault, the
website and the marketing repo fired the new CRIT rules 35 times in total, and every hit read as a
real tic. Four dev-blog strings ("sane defaults", "zero config", "zero-config", "batteries
included") were demoted to SOFT in that backtest, because Airflow `default_args` advice and a
release note for a cache store both used them literally and correctly.

Two writer-facing gaps closed with them. `rules_prompt.py` never rendered the tics, so the gate
blocked shapes the generated block in `CLAUDE.md` never named, and the banned headings had the same
problem. Both now render, and `TIC_DESCRIPTIONS` in `slop_rules.py` carries the plain-English form
of every tic. `rules_prompt.py` exits with an error when a tic has no description, so a new regex
cannot ship invisible to the writer.

One item was deliberately left out. The source list flags a colon opening onto three or more
items ("separate ports, processes, and local state") and says so itself: noisy in technical
writing, off by default for a documentation corpus. Section 4 already states the opposite case as
correct here ("A colon is correct before a list or an example"), and this vault's own prose uses
that construction constantly and on purpose. Banning it would fail correct writing, so it stays a
human judgement call, not a scorer rule.

## Related

- [Runtime contract](./runtime-contract.md), the load order and the checks
- [AI Writing Policy](../AI%20Writing%20Policy.md), the top directive
- [Voice](../Voice.md), how the writing sounds
- [Technical Writing Style Guide](../Technical%20Writing%20Style%20Guide.md), the technical layer

title: "Long-Form Writing Rules"
description: "The craft layer for long-form: essays, Substack articles, guides."
created: 2026-07-22
updated: 2026-08-07
---

# Long-Form Writing Rules

[AI Writing Policy](./AI%20Writing%20Policy.md) is the central directive and outranks this file. Read it first. Banned words, AI-tells, and the em-dash ban live in [Voice](./Voice.md) and apply here in full. Audience lives in [Audience](./Audience.md). This file is the craft layer: how to structure and pace a long piece, not what to cover. It is the canonical source for the craft rules, the four beats, and the headline. Skills reference it rather than restating it.

## The craft rules

1. **Lead with the reader's problem.** A section's first sentence names what they are stuck on, in their words. What you are explaining enters by sentence three at the earliest.
2. **One claim per sentence.** Split compounds joined by "and", "but", or a comma splice. Two short sentences beat one long one.
3. **Tables for three or more comparable items.** Options, tools, numbers, steps. AI search engines pull tables out intact. Prose lists get mangled. Bullets are fine for parallel items that are not strictly comparable.
4. **Real nouns beat adjectives.** "Cut the build from 20 minutes to 2", not "much faster". Name the customer, not a wall of logos. Every claim-making paragraph needs a name, number, date, or example. If you cannot add one, the claim is too vague to ship.
5. **End each section with a plain takeaway.** The last line or the bold lead says what to remember. This section's conclusion, not a tease for the next. No takeaway means the section is not earning its place.
6. **Headings short, literal, scannable.** 2 to 6 plain words. Not a thesis, metaphor, or clever line.

   | Instead of | Write |
   |---|---|
   | "What each metric tells you that a total cannot" | "Two signals a total hides" |
   | "A system your team can leave running" | "Leave it running" |
   | "Why the savings show up as a range and not a point" | "Why savings are a range" |
   | "The fear of regression is what keeps this switched off" | "Why teams leave it off" |

7. **Short sentences, small chunks.** Most under 22 words. Paragraphs of 1 to 3 sentences. Parallel points become bullets, steps become a numbered list.
8. **Build the piece on four beats, in order.** Every section sits on one of these or gets cut.

   | Beat | What it does |
   |---|---|
   | Calm story | Open far from the theory on a concrete moment or piece of history. Zero-effort entry, and the reader acclimatizes to the voice. "A report that used to build in two minutes now takes twenty." |
   | Plunge | Turn that opening upside down with the problem, the uncomfortable truth, or the paradox. Tension is the only thing keeping the reader on the page. |
   | Solution | The framework or rule arrives as the tool that gets them out. |
   | Higher ground | End above where the piece started. The reader closes it better equipped. |

9. **Bold lead-in bullets.** A bold 2-to-4-word label, then the explanation, so the reader scans labels first.
   - **They are dense.** One page can carry a dozen nested points.
   - **They are inconsistent.** Every source formats things differently.
10. **Plain sentence first, detail second.** Analogy when it helps. For unfamiliar areas open with a concepts table: term, what it is, why it matters here.
11. **Density is the metric, never length.** A clean 900-word piece stretched to 2,000 has readmitted every scrap of fluff you cut.
12. **Vary paragraph length on purpose.** A one-line paragraph speeds the reader up, a three-to-four-sentence block slows them down for a harder idea. Alternate deliberately. Never put every sentence on its own line: that is the LinkedIn robot look and it reads as cheap.
13. **Second draft equals first draft minus 10%.** Editing removes. Hunt the warm-up fluff up top, the middle sentence that repeats a made point, and the safe filler written while your brain warmed up.
14. **Contrast pairs and the witness rule.** Set a warm human word against a cold clinical one in adjacent clauses, so the reader feels the gap. Put yourself in as a witness to the argument, never its subject. One clean vignette anchors a claim. Venting does not.

**Captions do real work.** Image lead-ins and alt text say what is on screen and what it proves. Never "a screenshot of the dashboard".

**The digestibility test.** Could a smart newcomer skim the headings, bold bits, and lists and still get it? If not, cut and break up, without dropping a real number or name.

## The headline

Rule 6 governs section headings. The article headline is the opposite instinct: on a feed it carries most of the work, so it is outcome-driven, not topic-driven.

| Failure mode | Example | Why it dies |
|---|---|---|
| Poetic | "Sifting Through the Noise" | Meaningless at scroll speed |
| Dry textbook | "An Analysis of High-Growth Newsletter Models in 2026" | Reads like homework |
| Turned-up and honest | "I Analyzed 1,000 Short Posts. Here Are the 3 Layouts That Actually Get Free Sign-ups." | Exact metric, named headache, sounds like a smart friend |

All four at once where the character budget allows.

1. **A real number, timeframe, or metric.** Digits stop a scrolling eye. Use the true number.
2. **Name the headache the reader skips.** State the outcome, not the subject.
3. **Text it to a smart friend** who has been losing sleep over that problem. SEO-robot voice reads as robot voice.
4. **The primary keyword survives, in the title itself.** The rule an outcome-driven rewrite breaks most often. "We Templated Everything. Output Tripled in 4 Months." dropped "marketing" and stopped being findable. "Marketing Templates Tripled Our Output in 4 Months." keeps number, outcome, and keyword in 51 characters. Every content word of `target_keywords[0]` belongs in `seo_title`, and the slug is not a substitute. If it will not fit in 60 characters, shorten the outcome, never the keyword.

**The three-question check, before you publish.** Answer all three in a note. What belief or status quo does this piece challenge? What value does it give the reader? What emotion should it trigger? Write the headline from the strongest answer. A headline that answers none of the three is an explainer title, and explainer titles such as "Everything I know about X" fell flat in the source test.

**Seen beats advised.** When the piece gives no direct value such as a guide, the headline should make the reader feel seen. Write it as a statement about the reader, not as advice to the reader. "The year is 2063 and you were never interesting" combined existential dread with the belief that most people think they are special, and it was that creator's most viral piece. Source: [Substack Tips - Liz Leatrice](../LIBRARY/Notes/Substack%20Tips%20-%20Liz%20Leatrice.md).

The dek promises the honest, slightly uncomfortable version of the idea. A dek that restates the headline wasted the slot.

Cut the warm-up intro. Paragraphs explaining why you decided to write the post are the most common draft defect. Drop the reader into the problem in sentence one.

`python SCRIPTS/substack/craft.py "<file>"` checks rules 8, 11, 12, the headline rules, and the warm-up intro.

## Voice

One expert talking to a peer. Second draft from a tired expert, not PR polish. Short sentences, real verbs, open on the reader's problem. Numbers exact and attributed, rounded only if the source rounded. Match source casing for product names and commands. Every sentence has a finite verb. No trailing "this will help you achieve X".

Have a spine. Take a position and defend it with a real reason. A piece that offends no one and surprises no one is the worst outcome. Boring is a defect, same as a typo.

## Scaling down (posts, notes, threads)

Under about 400 words, rules 3, 5, and 6 are optional and rule 8 compresses to two beats, the plunge and the higher ground. Rules 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and all of Voice always apply, plus everything in [Voice](./Voice.md). The headline section applies to anything carrying a title.

# Substack Publication Standard

Every post on blog.atharvashah.com meets the rules below, so the archive reads as one
publication rather than 81 separate experiments. The standard came out of a full audit on
2026-09-26 that found 38 duplicate images, 159 captions that only repeated a heading, 13 images
stranded after the closing links, and 0 external embeds in most posts.
`SCRIPTS/substack/post_qa.py` checks every rule here that a script can see, on the vault file and
on the live post, and the writing gate runs it on every write to `2_PUBLISHED`. Writing rules live in
`SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` and the `DIGITAL TWIN/core/` files, and this file never restates
them.

## Each Image Appears Once, Where the Paragraph Introduces It

1. One copy of any image per post. The same picture under two captions tells the reader the
   captions are wrong.
2. An image sits directly after the paragraph that introduces it. Nothing but the "read next"
   post cards goes after the closing **Related reading** line.
3. The INIT template owns three images: the banner, the hero cover and the footer. Never edit,
   caption or move them.
4. A markdown table stays a table in the vault and publishes as an `md_table.py` image. Never
   keep an old screenshot of the same table beside it.
5. Never hotlink an image from another site. Download it into `META/Attachments/<url_slug>/`
   and let the CLI upload it, because hotlinks die. Two died in the gaming post before 2026-09-26.

## A Caption Says What the Reader Sees and Why It Matters

One sentence, 20 words or fewer. A screenshot names the tool or view and the detail to notice. A
diagram or chart states its takeaway, not its topic. A still or cover names the work, the studio
and the year. A table image carries no caption, because its header row does that job. A caption
never repeats the section heading and never carries an "image 2" label. The caption lives in the
vault as the image's alt text, `![caption](path)`, so it survives every push.

## Embeds Give the Reader Something the Paragraph Cannot

| Post length | Embeds |
|---|---|
| Under 1,000 words | 1 to 2 |
| 1,000 to 2,500 words | 4 to 5 |
| Over 2,500 words | 7 to 8 |

The counts are a ceiling for weak material, never a quota. An embed is the primary source of a
claim, the person or tool the paragraph names, a demo of the thing described, or a credible
counterpoint. Search in this order: Atharva's own X posts (one per post at most), accounts he
follows, first-party sources (the tool, the author, the studio), then other credible voices.

Three node types render as embed cards: an X post, a YouTube video and a Substack post (any
Substack newsletter). Verify every candidate before inserting it, because Substack hydrates each
one from the platform and a fake URL fails:

```bash
python SCRIPTS/substack/live_edit.py plan.json            # dry run hydrates every embed
```

An embed may carry one lead-in sentence of 20 words or fewer that names the speaker. Never
place two embeds side by side, and never embed the same URL in two posts.

## Diagrams Come From the Diagram Engine

Every flowchart, comparison, stack, cycle or architecture figure is built in
[`_DIAGRAM-ENGINE/`](./_DIAGRAM-ENGINE/README.md) from HTML, in the shared print style, and never
from an image model. Screenshots, photos and film stills stay as they are.

## Headings State a Claim in AP Title Case

Every H2 is AP Title Case and states what its section proves. The title of a book, film or game
goes in italics, `*The Graduate*`, which keeps its own capitals under the case check. The first
word after a colon or a leading number takes a capital. `SCRIPTS/slop/heading_case.py` enforces
all three.

## A Reader Who Was Not in the Room Still Follows the Post

Gloss an owned or niche term where it first appears: ICP, flywheel, harness, second brain, slop,
a product name such as Magi, AccuKnox or Jev, and an acronym such as CNAPP. A parenthesis or a
short naming clause is enough. `SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py` finds the misses.

## Edit a Live Post Surgically, Then Mirror the Vault

`SCRIPTS/substack/live_edit.py` changes a live post node by node: remove, caption, insert,
move, replace an image, set a heading, replace text. It targets nodes by content, backs up the
full record to `_LINK-ENGINE/backups/`, and re-reads the post to confirm the body, `post_date`,
email state, slug and title. Use it for any fix smaller than a rewrite, and never use
`substack.py update` for one, because update regenerates the whole body.

Make the same change in the vault copy in the same session. Embeds and other editor-only blocks
are preserved by `update` next to the paragraph they follow, so the vault records each one as a
comment on its own line after that paragraph, for example
`<!-- substack youtube2 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ID -->`. Run
`python SCRIPTS/substack/sync_audit.py audit "<file>"` afterwards. It must print 0 posts needing
attention.

def md_to_doc(md_text, md_path=None, cfg=None, with_images=True):
    """Convert markdown to a ProseMirror doc. Local images get uploaded to
    Substack's CDN when with_images is True and cfg is provided."""
    lines = md_text.split("\n")
    doc, i, n = [], 0, len(lines)
    skipped_images, skipped_html, skipped_tables = [], [], []
    skipped_comments = []

    while i < n:
        stripped = lines[i].strip()
        if stripped == "":
            i += 1
            continue

        # An HTML comment must never reach a reader. The html branch below does
        # not catch it, because its regex demands a letter or slash after the
        # angle bracket, so before 2026-08-09 every `<!-- substack node not
        # representable -->` marker fell through to the paragraph branch and got
        # published as literal text across 38 live posts. Swallow the whole
        # comment, including the multi-line case.
        if stripped.startswith("<!--"):
            start = i
            while i < n and "-->" not in lines[i]:
                i += 1
            skipped_comments.append(lines[start].strip()[:90])
            i += 1
            continue

        # Raw HTML has no ProseMirror equivalent. Falling through to the
        # paragraph branch publishes the literal tag as visible body text, which
        # is exactly what happened to a <video> tag on post 196324873. Skip it
        # loudly instead: a caller who sees the warning can decide what to do.
        if re.match(r"^<(/?)([a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*)\b[^>]*>", stripped):
            skipped_html.append(stripped)
            i += 1
            continue

        img = re.match(r"^!\[([^\]]*)\]\(([^\)]+)\)\s*$", stripped)
        if img:
            alt, src = img.group(1), img.group(2)
            if with_images and cfg and md_path and not src.startswith("http"):
                from urllib.parse import unquote
                local = (md_path.parent / unquote(src)).resolve()
                if local.exists():
                    url = upload_image(cfg, local)
                    doc.append(captioned_image(url, alt))
                    print(f"  uploaded image: {local.name}")
                else:
                    skipped_images.append(src)
            elif src.startswith("http"):
                doc.append(captioned_image(src, alt))
            else:
                skipped_images.append(src)
            i += 1
            continue

        if re.match(r"^(-{3,}|\*{3,})$", stripped):
            doc.append({"type": "horizontal_rule"})
            i += 1
            continue

        hm = re.match(r"^(#{1,6})\s+(.*)$", stripped)
        if hm:
            level = min(len(hm.group(1)), 3)
            doc.append({"type": "heading", "attrs": {"level": level},
                        "content": parse_inline(hm.group(2))})
            i += 1
            continue

        if stripped.startswith("```"):
            lang = stripped[3:].strip()
            code_lines = []
            i += 1
            while i < n and not lines[i].strip().startswith("```"):
                code_lines.append(lines[i])
                i += 1
            i += 1
            text = "\n".join(code_lines)
            doc.append({"type": "code_block", "attrs": {"language": lang or None},
                        "content": [{"type": "text", "text": text}] if text else []})
            continue

        # Substack's schema has no table node, so a markdown table published as
        # text collapses into one paragraph of pipes. Render it to a PNG instead.
        # The markdown stays in the vault; only the reader sees a picture.
        if stripped.startswith("|"):
            import md_table
            rows, j = md_table.parse_table(lines, i)
            if rows:
                if with_images and cfg:
                    try:
                        png = md_table.table_png(rows)
                        url = upload_image(cfg, png)
                        doc.append(captioned_image(url, ""))
                        print(f"  rendered table ({len(rows)}x{len(rows[0])}) "
                              f"-> {png.name}")
                    except Exception as e:
                        skipped_tables.append(f"{len(rows)}x{len(rows[0])}: {e}")
                else:
                    skipped_tables.append(f"{len(rows)}x{len(rows[0])} table")
                i = j
                continue

        if stripped.startswith(">"):
            q = []
            while i < n and lines[i].strip().startswith(">"):
                q.append(re.sub(r"^>\s?", "", lines[i].strip()))
                i += 1
            doc.append({"type": "blockquote", "content": [
                {"type": "paragraph", "content": parse_inline(" ".join(q))}]})
            continue

        for marker, ordered in ((r"^[-*]\s+", False), (r"^\d+\.\s+", True)):
            if re.match(marker, stripped):
                items = []
                while i < n and re.match(marker, lines[i].strip()):
                    items.append(re.sub(marker, "", lines[i].strip()))
                    i += 1
                doc.append({"type": "ordered_list" if ordered else "bullet_list",
                            "content": [{"type": "list_item", "content": [
                                {"type": "paragraph", "content": parse_inline(t)}]}
                                for t in items]})
                break
        else:
            para = [stripped]
            i += 1

3:title: Substack — Publishing Pipeline
4:description: "The content production engine. Ideas enter at the top, published articles exit at the bottom, the Socials flywheel fires right after."
9:# Substack — Publishing Pipeline
11:The content production engine. Ideas enter at the top, polished articles exit at the bottom, and the Socials flywheel fires immediately after publishing.
13:> **Standard:** [PUBLICATION STANDARD](./PUBLICATION%20STANDARD.md) is the bar every post meets for images, captions, embeds, diagrams and headings.
15:> **Related:** [Content Flywheel Plan for 2026](./2_PUBLISHED/Content%20Flywheel%20Plan%20for%202026.md) (the strategic blueprint), [Goals](../DIGITAL%20TWIN/Goals.md) (OKRs this system serves), [Voice](../DIGITAL%20TWIN/Voice.md) (the style every article must follow), [Audience](../DIGITAL%20TWIN/Audience.md) (who we write for), [[Content Sources]] (where ideas come from), [Substack Growth Checklist 2026](./GROWTH%20STRATEGY/Substack%20Growth%20Checklist%202026.md) (growth tactics)
19:## Architecture at a Glance
25:## Folder Structure
29:├── README.md                         ← This file (schema, SEO, sitemap SOP)
30:├── sitemap.md                        ← Generated: live post titles + URLs (deterministic pull)
32:├── _COVERS/                          ← All hero covers, flat: <url_slug>-cover.png
35:├── 2_PUBLISHED/                      ← Source of truth for all published content
39:`sitemap.md` comes from `python SCRIPTS/substack/substack.py sitemap` and is never hand-edited. The SEO scorecard is not a file: `python SCRIPTS/seo/audit.py` prints it to stdout on demand, so no stale report sits in the vault. Article images live in `META/Attachments/<url_slug>/`, not here.
45:## The Pipeline
48:[0_IDEAS] → DRAFT → [1_DRAFTS] → REVIEW → [2_PUBLISHED] → SOCIALS FLYWHEEL
51:**Half of everything published carries a video, set 2026-08-16.** The video goes at the top of the post and the article body goes underneath it. Someone who only watches and someone who only reads both get the whole argument, so neither half is a teaser for the other. Substack records it inside the editor, in the slot above the title field. The open questions on length, on scripting order, and on what the flywheel does with the footage live in item 16 of [TODO.md](./TODO.md).
53:### Phase 0. Triage (gate, before anything gets written)
55:79 published and 100 drafts is past the point where anyone remembers what is already covered, so every new idea gets checked against the corpus before it earns a file:
66:python SCRIPTS/substack/overlap.py thin     # published articles ranked by padding
67:python SCRIPTS/substack/overlap.py pairs    # published articles that duplicate each other
72:### Phase 1. Idea capture (`0_IDEAS/`)
74:Drop raw topics here. A title, a transcript, a URL, a brain dump. No format required, nothing in this folder is processed. Key files: `_Ideas To Process.md`, `_Ideas To Write.md`. Hand one off with `@substack-publisher develop [[Idea Title]] into a full draft`.
76:### Phase 2. Drafting (`1_DRAFTS/`)
84:type: Draft Article        # Idea -> Draft Article -> Article (lifecycle marker)
91:cover: "../_COVERS/<url_slug>-cover.png"   # hero image, named by slug
92:planned_date: 2026-08-15   # planned go-live (ideas/drafts) or real post date (published). Informational, nothing enforces it

### Phase 5. Publish and move (`2_PUBLISHED/`)

Publishing through the CLI (`substack.py push` then `publish`) handles the body, cover, subscribe widget, and comment button via the INIT template. If you instead publish by hand in the Substack web UI: paste the article, set title and subtitle, re-insert every image, verify formatting, add the subscribe CTA near the top, the soft share button mid-article, and the Comment button at the bottom.

Either way, finish the same:

1. Final review, then publish.
2. Move the file from `1_DRAFTS/` to `2_PUBLISHED/` with its live `ID` in frontmatter.
3. If the piece is part of a series, link to the previous and next parts. This is the only linking rule left and it is manual.
4. Trigger the flywheel: `@social-flywheel generate all social content for [[Article Title]]`.

---

## The `ID` Rule (gated)

An `ID` means "this exists on Substack." Ideas and drafts carry none until they are pushed, and `substack.py delete` strips the `ID` from the local file when it deletes the draft, so a dead ID can never linger. This matters because `push` reads a present `ID` as "update that draft" and would `PUT` to a deleted id instead of creating a new one.

Every article in `2_PUBLISHED/` must carry its live post ID. Without it nothing links the vault file back to the live post, so nothing can verify, resync, or update it, and drift goes undetected. `push` writes the ID automatically on first push. Backfill anything published outside the CLI:

```
python SCRIPTS/substack/check_ids.py             # check (offline, no network)
python SCRIPTS/substack/check_ids.py --fix       # resolve missing IDs from live by url_slug
python SCRIPTS/substack/check_ids.py --verify    # confirm each ID is live, report title drift
python SCRIPTS/substack/check_ids.py --sync-meta # pull live title/subtitle into seo_title/seo_description
```

The pre-commit hook runs `check_ids.py --staged` and blocks any commit putting an ID-less article into `2_PUBLISHED/`. It also fails when a file sits in `2_PUBLISHED/` with no matching live post, because that is a false claim about pipeline state. Publish it or move it back to `1_DRAFTS/`.

**Hooks live in `.githooks/`, not `.git/hooks/`.** This repo sets `core.hooksPath`, so git reads `.githooks/pre-commit` and ignores `.git/hooks/` completely. That directory is tracked, so hooks are version controlled and travel with a clone. A fresh clone sets the pointer once:

======
# Cover Engine

Deterministic Substack cover generator. HTML template, Playwright screenshot, no image model,
no manual export step. Every cover in the archive comes out of one file so the whole feed
reads as one publication.

Output is 1600x900 PNG at `out/<url_slug>-cover.png`, which is the exact filename
`SUBSTACK/_COVERS/` expects.

```bash
cd "D:\Atharva\NOTES\SUBSTACK\_COVER-ENGINE"
python render.py                       # every spec in covers.json -> out/
python render.py --only 50-ai          # one cover, slug substring match
python render.py --out ../_COVERS      # write straight into the live cover folder
python render.py --scale 2             # 3200x1800, for anything print or OG-large
```

---

## The strategy

### What makes Lenny's covers work

I pulled his last 30 thumbnails into `META/Attachments/lennys-podcast-thumbnails/` and took
them apart. Five things do all the work, and only one of them is the color.

1. **One background hue, speckled.** A radial gradient from a pale corner to a saturated
   corner, with a printed fleck texture over it. The grain is what stops it reading as a CSS
   gradient.
2. **Torn white paper blocks behind the headline.** One block per line, each rotated less than
   half a degree, each with a ragged edge. This is the single most recognizable element.
3. **Black grotesque at maximum weight.** Tight leading, negative tracking, 3 or 4 words per
   line. Never a full sentence.
4. **One subject on the right, bleeding off the edge.** For him it is a guest portrait. It
   fills roughly 40 percent of the canvas.
5. **A fixed furniture grid.** Logo top right, name and role bottom left, in the same place
   every single time. The grid is the brand. The color is just the label.

### What I changed for you

**The color question you asked.** Not blue, and not one flat color either. Here is the reasoning.
Lenny gets away with a single orange because his taxonomy is flat: every post is one podcast
episode. You publish across eight sections, so color is free information you are currently
throwing away. And your brand color is already a red-orange, so copying his orange would make
your covers look like his covers rather than like yours.

So: **the structure is the constant, the hue is the variable, and the red is reserved.** All
eight hues run through one recipe (same saturation curve, same lightness curve, same gradient
angle, same grain), which is what makes them feel like siblings instead of a rainbow. Hues 0 to
30 are off limits for backgrounds, which keeps the red wordmark legible on every single cover.

**The subject slot.** You have no guest to photograph, so the right side holds one large object
chosen for the topic. Four modes feed that one slot, which is the part that took the most
thought and is documented in full below.

**The human anchor.** Your LinkedIn photo sits in the bottom-left byline at 104px, keyed off
its blue studio backdrop and composited onto an off-white medallion so it works on all eight
hues. That is the slot Lenny uses for the guest's face and name. Yours never changes, which
over an archive of 150 covers is a feature.

**The byline.** Name in Inter 800, then the category as an uppercase tracked label in a dark
shade of the cover's own hue, a thin vertical rule, then the domain in regular weight at 68
percent. The category and the URL do different jobs, so they get different type instead of
being run together after a bullet.

**The watermark.** White pill, top right, brand mark plus the red `ATHARVA SHAH` wordmark.
Fixed size, fixed position, never varies.

### Why HTML and not an image model

Three reasons that matter more than the render quality.

- **Reproducible.** Change one palette value and all 151 covers regenerate identically. An
  image model gives you a different cover every time you run it.
- **Text is real text.** No mangled letterforms, no misspellings, no "almost the right font".
  The headline is Inter 900 vector type, screenshotted.
- **Zero cost per cover, zero API.** Runs offline. Fonts and subjects are vendored locally, so
  a render works with no network at all.

---

## The safe zone, which is the rule that breaks covers

Output is **2400x1350** (16:9). Substack renders that same file three different ways and
only one of them shows the whole frame.

| Surface | What it fetches | Ratio | What it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open Graph, which is LinkedIn | `w_1200,h_675,c_fill` on the cover | 1.7778 | nothing, full 16:9 |
| Archive and feed cards | `c_fill` at `w_960,h_639` plus four smaller sizes | 1.5023 | 124px off each side |
| The X card | `api/v1/post_preview/<id>/twitter.jpg`, a Substack-generated 1600x800 | 2.0 | 80px each side, 80 top, 100 bottom |

Measured, not guessed. The archive figure comes from the `c_fill` params in the archive page
HTML. The X figure came from solving for the crop rectangle by correlating a published cover
against its own `twitter.jpg`, which lands on **x [56, 1544], y [80, 824]** in 1600-space and
repeats across posts.

The intersection is **x = [124, 1476], y = [80, 800]**, and every visible element lives inside
it: headline at left 130 top 92, byline at left 134 bottom 108, wordmark pill at right 130 top
96, and the tile at right 106 bottom 148 shrunk to 460 so the headline box stays at 924px. The
outer bands are background and nothing else, ever.

The first version of this engine put the headline at x=62 y=54 and the wordmark at x=1554. The
archive page chopped the first letter off every headline, and the X card cut the wordmark in
half and sliced the byline. Both are fixed.

`python measure_fit.py` asserts the box on all four edges and exits non-zero on a breach, so
the rule is enforced rather than remembered.

### The X card cache, which cannot be purged

`twitter:image` points at a Substack-generated card, not at the cover, and there is no lever
to force it.

- The URL ends in `?version=4`, and that number is **4 on every post in the publication**. It
  is Substack's card template version, not a per-post cache key, so it never moves when a
  cover changes.
- `PUT /api/v1/posts/{id}/clear_cache` returns 403 with the publication cookie and 404 on the
  substack.com hub.
- Origin sends `Cache-Control: no-cache`, and CloudFront serves `X-Cache: Hit` regardless.

content.content:
## Spec format

`covers.json` is an array. One object per cover.

```json
{
  "slug": "50-ai-terms-for-professional-vibe-coders-and-devs",
  "category": "AI",
  "lines": ["50 AI terms", "you actually", "need"],
  "subject": "robot.svg",
  "seed": 3
}
```

| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `slug` | yes | must equal the article's `url_slug`, becomes `<slug>-cover.png` |
| `category` | yes | one of the eight keys above |
| `lines` | yes | 2 to 4 strings, 3 is the sweet spot, keep each under 14 characters |
| `subject` | yes | filename in `subjects/` |
| `seed` | no | integer, shifts the grain so no two covers share a texture |
| `subjectMode` | no | `tile` (default), `glyph`, or `plain` |
| `glyph` | glyph mode only | the string to set, 2 to 4 characters |
| `fontSize` | no | px, overrides headline autofit |
| `subjectWidth` | no | px, default 560 in tile mode and 660 in plain |
| `subjectScale` | no | percent of the tile the mark fills, default 64 |

### Writing the lines

The headline on the cover is not the article title. It is the sharpest 5 to 8 words in the
piece, broken where a person would breathe. Three rules:

- Break on meaning, never to fill the block. `"50 AI terms" / "you actually" / "need"` works
  because each fragment is readable alone.
- **Keep every line at 14 characters or under.** This is the one rule that controls how big the
  type comes out. The autofit shrinks on the widest line, so a single 18-character line drags the
  whole headline down by 40 or 50px. `"Loop engineering" / "is not new"` rendered at 100px.
  Re-broken to `"Loop" / "engineering" / "is not new"` it renders at 152px, with the same words.
  Four short lines always beat two long ones. Run `measure_fit.py` if you want the number.
- Numbers and dollar figures earn their own line. They are the reason someone stops scrolling.
- No banned patterns from `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py`. `"X, not Y"` is out, and it is the
  shape a cover headline falls into most easily.

## The subject slot

An emoji pack is a closed vocabulary of about 1,500 concrete nouns. It has no companies, no
tools, no niche technical objects. There is no Anthropic emoji and there never will be, so a
system built only on emoji breaks on the first post about a named product.

The fix is that the right side is a **slot with four modes**, not one image source. Every mode
renders into the same 660px square in the same position, so the archive stays uniform no matter
where the artwork came from.

| Mode | What it holds | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `tile` (default) | any mark or icon on a white app-icon squircle | everything, brand or concept |
| `glyph` | oversized Inter 900 type on the same squircle | a number or short string is the story: `48K`, `9x9`, `$0` |
| `plain` | a full-bleed object with no backing, running off the corner | only a real photographic cutout |

The white squircle is the wrapper for every subject, and that is the whole trick. Brand marks
are flat and usually near black, so on a saturated background they either vanish or look pasted
on. Put one on a squircle at 64 percent and it reads as an app icon, which is a deliberate
object. Run the same wrapper around a colour emoji and the two are visibly siblings, which is
what stops a feed of 150 covers from looking like a scrapbook.

`plain` exists for the one case the tile cannot hold: a real cutout photograph, which has an
organic silhouette and wants to bleed off the corner the way Lenny's portraits do. Do not use it
for icons.

`glyph` is the escape hatch. When no icon set has the thing, the number usually is the thing.

### Fetching

One helper, one endpoint. Iconify aggregates roughly 200,000 icons across 150 sets, including
`logos` (1,900 full-colour brand marks), `fluent-emoji`, `noto`, `flat-color-icons`,
`skill-icons`, and `devicon`.

```bash
python fetch_subject.py anthropic                     # picks logos:anthropic-icon
python fetch_subject.py "neural network" --list        # inspect candidates first
python fetch_subject.py openai --pick logos:openai-icon --name openai
```

It prints the spec line to paste, and tells you when the source is monochrome and therefore
needs `tile` mode. The set priority ladder inside the script is ordered by how well each set
survives at 500px on a coloured background, which is why every monochrome line-icon set ranks
last: a 2px stroke disappears at cover size.

Vendored so far: robot, brain, palette, chart, moneybag, briefcase, clapper, globe, book,
rocket, bulb, laptop, bullseye, anthropic, dbt, neural-network.

## The whole-archive run

Done on 2026-08-02. All 155 articles across `0_IDEAS`, `1_DRAFTS` and `2_PUBLISHED` now carry a
generated cover. The 151 covers that predated the system were kept in `SUBSTACK/_COVER-ARCHIVE/`
until 2026-08-08, when that folder was deleted. Recover any of them from git history if needed.

The pipeline, in the order it runs:

1. `inventory.json` is scraped from the frontmatter of every article: folder, file, `url_slug`,
   `seo_title`, `seo_description`, `category`, `cover`.
2. `headlines.tsv` is the hand-written layer, one line per article:
   `slug` tab `bucket` tab `icon` tab `line|line|line`. This is the only file that needs human
   judgement, because a cover headline is not a title and cannot be derived from one.
3. `python build_specs.py` validates and emits `covers-all.json`. It fails loudly on an unknown
   slug, an article with no headline, a missing icon file, a bad bucket, or a line over 20
   characters. Nothing renders until it passes.
4. `python render.py --spec covers-all.json` writes 155 PNGs to `out/`.
5. Publishing copies `out/` into `_COVERS/` and rewrites each article's `cover:` frontmatter to
   `../_COVERS/<url_slug>-cover.png`. Orphaned covers are deleted, and git history is the only
   backup now that `_COVER-ARCHIVE/` is gone.

To regenerate one article, edit its line in `headlines.tsv`, then:

```bash
python build_specs.py && python render.py --spec covers-all.json --only <slug> --out ../_COVERS
```

### A brand-new article has no cover yet

Step 1 above happened once, on 2026-08-02. There is no `build_inventory.py` in this repo, so
`inventory.json` is not re-scraped on every run. A new article's slug is unknown to
`build_specs.py` until you add it by hand:

1. Append an entry to `inventory.json`: `{"folder", "file", "slug", "title", "desc", "category",
   "cover"}`, where `cover` is `../_COVERS/<slug>-cover.png`. Copy the shape of any existing row.
2. Add its `headlines.tsv` line, same as regenerating one article above. Pick `bucket` and `icon`
   by grepping `headlines.tsv` for a similar existing article, since the convention is not
   written down anywhere else, for example every Claude Code piece uses `AI` and `anthropic`.
3. Run the same two commands as regenerating one article.

Skipping step 1 is why `check_covers.py`, the pre-commit gate, blocks with "cover path does not
match its url_slug" on a first-time article even though the frontmatter `cover:` line looks
correct.

def cmd_push(cfg, args):
    path = Path(args.file).resolve()
    if not path.exists():
        die(f"file not found: {path}")
    fm, body_md = read_frontmatter(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    title = article_title(fm, path)
    subtitle = article_subtitle(fm)
    draft_id = fm.get("ID")
    slug = require_slug(fm, path)   # fail before uploading anything

    print(f"converting: {path.name}")
    doc = md_to_doc(body_md, md_path=path, cfg=cfg, with_images=not args.no_images)

    cover_url = None if args.no_images else push_cover(cfg, fm, path)
    if not args.no_template:
        doc = wrap_in_template(cfg, doc, cover_url)

    # `slug` is deliberately NOT in this payload. Substack 400s on a slug it
    # already owns, so it is written only when it differs. See enforce_slug.
    payload = {"draft_title": title, "draft_subtitle": subtitle,
               "draft_body": json.dumps(doc)}
    payload.update(seo_meta_payload(fm))
    if cover_url:
        payload["cover_image"] = cover_url
    if draft_id:
        api(cfg, "PUT", f"/drafts/{draft_id}", payload)
        enforce_slug(cfg, draft_id, slug, "push")
        print(f"updated draft {draft_id}: {title}")
    else:
        payload.update({"draft_bylines": [{"id": cfg["user_id"], "is_guest": False}],
                        "type": "newsletter", "audience": "everyone"})
        resp = api(cfg, "POST", "/drafts", payload)
        draft_id = resp["id"]
        write_id_to_frontmatter(path, draft_id)
        enforce_slug(cfg, draft_id, slug, "draft creation")
        print(f"created draft {draft_id}: {title} (ID written to frontmatter)")
    print(f"  slug: {slug}")
    print(f"edit at: {cfg['base'].replace('/api/v1', '')}/publish/post/{draft_id}")


# Node types md_to_doc can generate. Anything else in a live post's body was
# added in Substack's editor and cannot survive a regeneration from markdown.
MD_NODE_TYPES = {
    "doc", "paragraph", "heading", "code_block", "blockquote", "bullet_list",
    "ordered_list", "list_item", "horizontal_rule", "captionedImage", "image2",
    "text", "caption",
}

# Supplied by the INIT template on every push, so never worth preserving by
# hand. wrap_in_template puts them back.
TEMPLATE_NODE_TYPES = {"subscribeWidget", "ctaCaption", "button"}


def node_text(node):
    """Flattened text of a node, used as an anchor for re-splicing."""
    out = []

    def walk(n):
        if n.get("type") == "text":
            out.append(n.get("text", ""))
        for c in n.get("content", []) or []:
            walk(c)

    walk(node)
    return "".join(out).strip()


def extract_natives(body):
    """Top-level nodes markdown cannot rebuild, each tagged with the text of the
    preceding content block so it can be put back in the same place.

    Returns [(anchor_text, index, node)]. A video is a Substack media upload and
    a digestPostEmbed carries a whole hydrated payload; neither can be described
    in markdown, so preserving the node verbatim is the only way not to lose it.
    """
    natives, anchor = [], ""
    for idx, node in enumerate(body.get("content", []) or []):
        t = node.get("type")
        if t in TEMPLATE_NODE_TYPES:
            continue
        if t not in MD_NODE_TYPES:
            natives.append((anchor, idx, node))
            continue
        text = node_text(node)
        if text:
            anchor = text
    return natives


def splice_natives(doc, natives):
    """Re-insert preserved nodes after the paragraph they followed originally.

    Anchoring on text rather than index survives the body being rewritten around
    them. A native whose anchor no longer exists goes to the end, which is
    visible in the report rather than silently dropped."""
    content = list(doc.get("content", []))
    placed, orphaned = 0, []
    for anchor, idx, node in natives:
        target = None
        if anchor:
            key = anchor[:60]
            for i, n in enumerate(content):
                if node_text(n)[:60] == key:
                    target = i + 1
                    break
        if target is None:
            if not anchor:            # led the article, so put it back on top
                target = 0
            else:
                orphaned.append(node.get("type"))
                target = len(content)
        content.insert(target, node)
        placed += 1
    return {"type": "doc", "content": content}, placed, orphaned


def native_blocks(body_json):
    """Count node types in a Substack body that markdown cannot express."""
    counts = {}

    def walk(node):
        if isinstance(node, dict):
            t = node.get("type")
            if t and t not in MD_NODE_TYPES:
                counts[t] = counts.get(t, 0) + 1
            for child in node.get("content", []) or []:
                walk(child)
        elif isinstance(node, list):
            for child in node:
                walk(child)

    try:
        walk(json.loads(body_json))
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        pass
    return counts


def cmd_update(cfg, args):
    """Rewrite an already-published post from its vault file and push it live.

    Publishing a post splits it in two: the live title/subtitle/body readers
    see, and the draft_* staging copy. 'push' writes only the staging copy, so
    it never changes the public page. This writes staging, then re-publishes
    with send=false to copy staging over live. post_date and email_sent_at are
    left alone, so no feed bump and no email."""
    path = Path(args.file).resolve()
    if not path.exists():
        die(f"file not found: {path}")
    fm, body_md = read_frontmatter(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    post_id = fm.get("ID")
    if not post_id:
        in_published = "2_PUBLISHED" in path.parts
        hint = ("python SCRIPTS/substack/check_ids.py --fix"
def cmd_publish(cfg, args):
    if not args.yes:
        die("publish goes live IMMEDIATELY (the API ignores future dates). "
            "Rerun with --yes to confirm.")
    d = api(cfg, "GET", f"/drafts/{args.id}")

    # The vault owns the public URL. Publishing is the last moment to assert
    # it, because after this the slug is frozen and the old URL 404s with no
    # redirect.
    local = find_by_id(args.id)
    want = None
    if local:
        fm, _ = read_frontmatter(local.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        want = require_slug(fm, local)
        # A live post must never link to an article that is not live. The link
        # would 404 the moment a reader clicks it.
        require_links_publishable(local)
        if d.get("slug") != want:
            api(cfg, "PUT", f"/drafts/{args.id}", {"slug": want})
            print(f"  slug set from {local.name}: {want}")
    else:
        print(f"  WARNING: no vault file claims ID {args.id}, so the slug "
              f"cannot be verified against local frontmatter.")

    resp = api(cfg, "POST", f"/drafts/{args.id}/publish",
               {"send": not args.no_email, "share_automatically": False})
    print(f"PUBLISHED {args.id}: {d.get('draft_title')}"
          f" (email {'sent' if not args.no_email else 'skipped'})")
    slug = enforce_slug(cfg, args.id, want, "publish") if want else resp.get("slug")
    if slug:
        print(f"live at: {cfg['base'].replace('/api/v1', '')}/p/{slug}")
    try:
        count = refresh_sitemap(cfg)
        print(f"sitemap refreshed ({count} posts)")

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/write-for-one-reader.md -->
# Write for One Reader and One Claim

Name the one reader before you draft, and decide the one claim they carry away. "Load order decides which rule wins" is a claim. "Load order" is a subject.

## Why

A piece for everyone reads as a piece for no one.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/opening-earns-the-second-sentence.md -->
# The Opening Earns the Second Sentence

Write the first sentence so the reader wants the second one.

## Why

The first sentence is the only one every reader sees.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/each-paragraph-answers-the-last.md -->
# Each Paragraph Answers the Last

Make each paragraph answer a question the paragraph before it raised. Cut or move a paragraph that answers nothing.

## Why

A paragraph that answers nothing is a note, and notes break the thread.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/take-a-position-then-its-limit.md -->
# Take a Position, Then State Its Limit

Take a position, then say where it is weak.

## Why

A claim with no limit reads as marketing. The limit is what a practitioner trusts you for.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/rewrite-by-cutting.md -->
# Rewrite by Cutting, Not Smoothing

Rewrite by cutting and reordering, never by smoothing.

## Why

---
type: Vault Guide
title: Substack Diagram Engine
description: "Every explanatory figure on the Substack is built here from HTML, in one shared print style. Never from an image model."
created: 2026-09-26
updated: 2026-09-26
---

# Substack Diagram Engine

Every diagram inside a Substack article is an HTML fragment rendered to PNG by this folder.
One stylesheet, `figure.css`, holds the whole visual system, so two figures in two posts look
like one publication made them. An image model never draws a diagram here, because it
misspells labels and invents icons. Screenshots, photos and film stills are never redrawn.

```bash
python SUBSTACK/_DIAGRAM-ENGINE/render.py figures/<name>.html
python SUBSTACK/_DIAGRAM-ENGINE/render.py --all
```

The PNG lands in `out/<name>.png` at 2000 px wide, which Substack shows at 728 px. Copy it to
`META/Attachments/<url_slug>/` and embed it like any other image. The renderer prints `LINT` and
exits 1 when text overflows a box, boxes overlap, or a box leaves the frame.

## The Look Matches the TLDR One-Pager Sheets

The tokens are the same ones the `tldr` skill uses, so a summary sheet and an in-article
diagram read as the same publication.

| Role | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Paper | `#fbfaf6` | Figure ground, always opaque, with a 1 px hair frame |
| Ink | `#15140f` | Text, box strokes, arrows, step circles, label chips |
| Panel | `#f2f0e8` | Neutral box fill |
| Band | `#e9e6da` | A grouping zone behind several boxes |
| Yellow | `#fbeb9f` | The one box or phrase the reader must look at |
| Gold | `#b8944d` | The result or end state, used once |
| Blue, red, green | pale fill plus dark stroke | Second axis only: new vs old, fail vs pass |
| Muted | `#6e6b60` | Kicker, notes, source line |

Type is Source Serif 4 for titles and body, Inter for box labels, chips and numbers. The title
is 34 px, box labels 19 px, box text 18 px, and nothing drops below 13 px. At 728 px on the page
that keeps box text near 13 px, which the research below sets as the floor.

The figure never ships with a transparent background. Black ink on a transparent PNG vanishes in
the Substack app's dark mode, and a baked paper ground with a hair frame reads as a print card
on both white and dark readers.

## Nine Rules Every Figure Follows

1. **The title states the claim.** "One market is one campaign, and every campaign fills the
   same slots" works. "Knowledge base structure" is a topic and fails.
2. **The dek gives the frame in one or two sentences,** including any owned term the reader
   needs, such as "ICP (ideal customer profile)".
3. **About 50 words of box text, 80 at most.** Past that, split the figure.
4. **At most 7 nodes in a flow, 6 spokes on a hub, 4 kinds of node.** More categories than
   that stops being readable at a glance.
5. **One accent.** Yellow marks the part the claim is about. Gold marks the result, once.
6. **Label on the shape, never in a legend.** If a colour needs a legend, remove the colour.
7. **Flows read left to right, then top to bottom.** Only a cycle has an arrow that points back.
8. **Every box traces to a real step, file or component.** A box named "Orchestration Layer"
   names nothing a reader can check.
9. **No icons, gradients, glow, shadows or 3D.** A shape is a rectangle, a pill or a chip.

## A Small Class Set Builds Every Figure

A fragment is `<div id="fig" data-wires='[...]'>` with a `.kicker`, `.title`, `.dek`, a
`.canvas` holding the boxes, and a `.source` line. Boxes are `.node` with `.h` (label) and
`.p` (one line of detail). Variants: `.key` (yellow), `.result` (gold), `.plain`, `.ghost`
(dashed boundary), `.good`, `.bad`, `.pass`. A `.num` circle numbers a step. A `.chip` is a
black uppercase label, and `.band` groups boxes on a darker panel. Layout uses `.row`, `.col`
and `.grow`.

Arrows are declared in `data-wires`, never drawn by hand:

```json
[["fromId", "toId"], ["a", "b", {"label": "yes", "style": "dash", "from": "b", "to": "t"}]]
```

The renderer places them after layout, so moving a box never breaks an arrow. Styles are
